record.field: welcome start begin help getting started

div.p: Welcome! This system keeps track of everything the trust buys and uses — feed, medicine, ghee for pooja, tools.
New here? Open the guides below in order. They use plain language and real examples.

ul.li: Stuck on a word? Search the Help Center (try "FIFO" or "compartment").
See a hint under a field? That is here to help — read it before you type.
Beginner Mode is ON for you, so you will see extra guidance. You can turn it off in your Preferences once you are comfortable.

record.field: fifo, first in first out, oldest stock, in_date, issue, rotation

p.b: FIFO means the oldest stock leaves the shelf first.

div.p: When you issue an item, the system looks at when each batch arrived (its "in-date") and gives you the oldest one first.
Why it matters Stock that sits too long goes stale, rusts, or gets forgotten at the back of a rack. FIFO keeps things moving in the order they came in, so nothing rots while newer stock gets used.

Real trust example You have two sacks of cattle feed: one received in January, one in March. When a helper does a Scan Issue, the system points them to the January sack first. The older feed gets used while it's still good, and the March sack waits its turn.
Good to know FIFO is the normal rule for most items. For things that can expire (medicine, feed, fluids, pooja items), the system uses a smarter rule called FEFO instead — see that article.

record.field: fefo, first expiry first out, expiry, medicine, feed, pooja, expiry date

div.p: FEFO means the item that expires soonest leaves the shelf first — even if a different batch arrived earlier.
The system uses FEFO automatically for anything that can go bad: medicine, feed, fluids, and pooja items, or any product that has an expiry date set.

Why it matters With ordinary FIFO you ship the oldest-arrived item. But a batch that arrived first might expire later than a batch that arrived second. FEFO fixes that: the soonest-to-expire goes out first, so medicine and feed are never wasted sitting on the shelf past their date.

Real trust example FEFO means the bottle of calcium that expires first leaves the shelf first — so medicine never expires unused. If you have one calcium batch expiring December 2026 and a newer-looking batch expiring June 2027, FEFO still hands you the December batch first.

Clever detail FEFO even looks across different batches of the same product name. If two deliveries of "Calcium Bolus" sit in different slots, the wizard will pull from the earlier-expiring slot first and tell you which slot to pick from.

record.field: rack, shelving, grid, shelf, column, storage, R01

div.p: A Rack is one shelving unit — like a single bookcase standing against the wall.
Each rack is laid out as a grid of shelves (the horizontal rows) and columns (the vertical strips). A new rack defaults to 6 shelves tall and 3 columns wide, but you can set any size.

Why it matters The rack is the top of the storage map. Every item ultimately lives somewhere on a rack's grid, so giving each rack a clear code (like R01 or PHARM01) is how a helper knows which piece of furniture to walk to.

Real trust example In the medicine room you might have a rack coded PHARM01. On its label-printed barcode it shows as R-PHARM01. A helper scans or reads that to confirm they're at the right rack before looking for the exact shelf and column.
Remember the family A Rack holds Compartments, and a Compartment holds Slots. So the full address of any item is: Rack → Compartment → Slot.

record.field: compartment, shelf column rectangle, grid, cubby, divider, SH01 C01

div.p: A Compartment is a rectangle on the rack's grid — one cubby, drawer, or boxed-off area where you actually put stock.

A compartment sits at a shelf-and-column position. It can be a single cell (SH01 C01), tall across several shelves (SH01-03 C01, good for tall bottles), wide across several columns (SH01 C01-03, good for a wide drawer), or a whole block (SH01-03 C01-03, a corner cabinet).

Why it matters The compartment is how you turn a big rack into clearly labelled spaces so two people store and find things the same way. "Shelf" and "column" are just grid coordinates — the compartment is the real spot.

Real trust example On rack PHARM01, the calcium bottles live in compartment PHARM01 / SH01-03 / C01 — a tall compartment spanning the top three shelves of the first column. Its name always starts with the rack code so it's never confused with a C01 on a different rack.
Note A compartment must sit inside a Rack, and it contains one or more Slots (usually just one).

record.field: slot, bin, location, holds stock, SL01, smallest unit

div.p: A Slot is the smallest storage spot — the exact place the stock physically sits. It's the bottom of the storage map.
Most compartments have just one slot (the compartment is the slot). But a compartment can be split into several slots if you want to subdivide it — slot 1, slot 2, and so on.

Why it matters The slot is what the system actually counts stock against. When you receive, issue, or count an item, you're really pointing at a slot. Its full name reads like an address: PHARM01 / SH01-03 / C01 / SL01.

Real trust example When a helper does a Scan Issue for calcium, the wizard tells them the exact slot to pick from: "take 2 from PHARM01 / SH01-03 / C01 / SL01." No guessing which shelf — the slot name walks them straight to it.
Also good to know Stock can also sit in a Floor / Open area (see that article) instead of a rack slot — for sacks, pallets, or yard items that don't fit on shelving.

record.field: zone, building, area, floor, group of racks, room

div.p: A Zone is a big area that groups several racks together — like a room, a building, or a section of the shed.
A zone doesn't hold stock itself. It's a label for a region so the racks inside it are organised and easy to find.

Why it matters As the trust grows, you may have racks in the medicine room, the feed store, and the tool shed. Zones let you say "everything in the Pharmacy Zone" or "everything in the Feed Store Zone" instead of hunting rack by rack.

Real trust example You might create a Pharmacy Zone that contains racks PHARM01 and PHARM02, and a separate Feed Store Zone for the feed racks. A new helper learning the layout first finds the right zone (room), then the rack, then the compartment and slot.
Tip Zones, racks, compartments, and slots are all set up by an Admin using the WMS Configuration menu (Create Rack / Generate Zones).

record.field: floor, open area, pallet, yard, sacks, bulk, open storage

div.p: A Floor location is open-area storage — a pallet spot, a floor stack, or an outside yard bay where stock sits directly on the ground, not on rack shelving.

Why it matters Not everything fits in a neat rack compartment. Big sacks of feed, drums of fluid, or bulky tools often live on the floor or on a pallet. A floor location lets the system track that stock just like a slot does.

Real trust example Twenty sacks of cattle feed arrive and won't fit on a shelf, so they go on a pallet in the feed store. That pallet is a Floor location. When a helper receives or issues feed, the system can point to the floor area exactly the way it points to a rack slot — and FIFO/FEFO still work.

Good to know Floor locations behave the same as slots for receiving, issuing, counting (cycle count), damage, and repair. The difference is only that there's no compartment/shelf/column above them — stock lands there directly.

record.field: quant, quantity record, stock at a location, on hand, in_date, batch

div.p: A Quant is one line of "this much of this product is sitting in this spot." It's how the system records stock.
Each quant remembers four things: which product, which slot (or floor), how many, and when it arrived (the in-date).

Why it matters Quants are the truth about your stock. Every count on a report, every FIFO pick, every "on-hand" number comes from adding up quants. You don't usually create quants by hand — they appear automatically when you receive, issue, or move stock.

Real trust example After receiving feed, the system creates a quant like: product = Cattle Feed, slot = Feed Store pallet, quantity = 20 sacks, in-date = 1 June. If a second delivery lands in March, that's a second quant for the same product — and FIFO uses each quant's in-date to decide which sack goes out first.
Plain version Think of a quant as one sticky note on one pile of stock, saying what it is, how much, and when it got here.

record.field: reserved, reserved quantity, allocated, set aside, free to use, in-flight issue

div.p: Reserved quantity is stock that's already been promised to an in-progress job — it's still physically on the shelf, but it's spoken for.
The stock you can actually take = on-hand minus reserved (the "free" amount).

Why it matters Without reservations, two helpers could grab the same units at the same time and the counts would go wrong. Reserving stock for an in-flight Scan Issue keeps everyone honest about what's truly available.

Real trust example A slot shows 5 bottles of medicine on-hand. One helper has started a Scan Issue for 3 bottles, so 3 are reserved. If you then try to file a Damage for 4 bottles from that slot, the system stops you: only 2 are free right now. You either wait for the first issue to finish or reduce your quantity.
Plain version On-hand = everything on the shelf. Reserved = the part already claimed. Free = what's left for you.

record.field: on hand, on-hand, current stock, available, total quantity, count

div.p: On-hand is how many units are physically present right now — the total sitting in a slot, a rack, or the whole warehouse.

Why it matters On-hand is the number you check before issuing, ordering, or counting. But be careful: on-hand includes stock that may already be reserved for another job. The amount you can freely take is on-hand minus reserved.

Real trust example A helper opens the calcium product and sees on-hand = 5. That's five bottles in the building. If three are already reserved for someone else's issue, only two are free to grab today. The location screen also shows on-hand per slot, so you can see exactly where those five bottles are split across racks.
Watch out for damaged/repair stock Items moved to the Damage or Repair area are no longer counted as usable on-hand — so the number you see for "what's available to issue" stays honest.

record.field: in date, in_date, arrival date, received date, age, fifo key

div.p: The In-date is the date and time a batch of stock arrived in the warehouse. The system stamps it automatically the moment you receive an item.

Why it matters The in-date is what makes FIFO work. To send the oldest stock out first, the system simply sorts by in-date and picks the earliest. It's also used to spot stock that has been sitting untouched for a long time.

Real trust example Two sacks of feed: one with in-date 1 January, one with in-date 1 March. When a helper issues feed, FIFO reads the in-dates and hands them the January sack first. Nobody has to remember which arrived first — the in-date does it.

ul.li: You don't type the in-date yourself; it's set when stock is received.
For items that expire, the system prefers the expiry date over the in-date (that's FEFO). The in-date is the tie-breaker when two batches share an expiry.

record.field: sku, stock keeping unit, internal reference, product code, naming, category-item-variant

div.p: A SKU is the short code that names a product — the trust's permanent nickname for one exact item.
The trust's format is CATEGORY-ITEM-VARIANT, always UPPERCASE, letters/numbers/hyphen only, 20 characters or fewer. Examples: RM-ASH-001, PK-JAR-500, TOOL-DRILL-18V, SPARE-BLT-M4.

Why it matters Names change and get messy ("Soap (new)", "soap big"). A SKU never changes, so searching, counting, ordering, and 5-year-old records all still line up. The first part also tells you what kind of thing it is: RM raw material, FL fluid, TOOL tool, SPARE spare part, and so on.
Real trust example Gingelly oil is FL-OIL-001. Type FL- into search and every fluid appears instantly. When you later add coconut oil, it becomes FL-OIL-COCO — same family, clearly different.

Golden rule Never rename an existing SKU — it breaks the history trail. If something genuinely changes, create a new SKU and archive the old one. The SKU is usually also printed as the product's barcode.

record.field: barcode, code128, ean-13, scanner, label, scan, product code, slot label

div.p: A barcode is a printed pattern of stripes that a scanner reads instantly, so you don't type codes by hand.
The system uses two common kinds:

ul.li: Code128 — the default. It can hold letters, numbers and hyphens, so it can print your full SKU like TOOL-DRILL-18V. Used for product labels and for slot/rack labels.
EAN-13 — the familiar 13-digit shop barcode already printed on many manufactured products (e.g. 8901234567890).

div.p: Why it matters Many helpers are temporary or low-tech, often working on a tablet. A scan beep is faster and far less error-prone than reading and typing a code, and it works the same on wired, wireless, or Bluetooth scanners (they all act like a keyboard).

Real trust example A medicine box already has an EAN-13 from the maker — scan it and the product pops up. Your own ash powder, which has no factory barcode, gets a printed Code128 label of its SKU RM-ASH-001. Either way, one scan finds the product. Slots and racks also carry barcodes (like R-PHARM01) so you can scan the location too.
Tip Set your scanner to add an "Enter" after each scan — that's the factory default and lets scans process automatically.

record.field: scan receipt, receiving, incoming, receive stock, delivery, qc, putaway

div.p: Scan Receipt is the screen you use to bring new stock into the warehouse. You scan each item, the system adds it to a list, and when you're done you press Validate.

How it works 1. Scan a product (or a carton barcode that counts as many units). It's added with a quantity. 2. Optionally scan a slot to say where it goes — or leave it and let the system auto-pick a spot ("putaway"). 3. Tick Quality check passed to confirm you counted and inspected the delivery. 4. Choose the on-duty Store Keeper and Validate. The stock lands in its slot with today's date as the in-date.
Why it matters Receiving is where good (or bad) data begins. A quick scan-and-check keeps counts accurate and records who received what, when, and from whom.

Real trust example A vendor drops off 24-bottle cartons of calcium. The helper scans the carton barcode (which adds 24 at once), repeats for each carton, ticks Quality check, picks their name as Store Keeper, and validates. The bottles are now on the shelf and findable by scan.

record.field: scan issue, issue, take out, fifo, fefo, withdraw, usage note, taken by

div.p: Scan Issue is the screen you use to take stock out for use. Since the trust uses inventory itself (it never sells), this is how feed, medicine, ghee, and tools leave the store for the cows, the pooja room, or a repair job.

How it works 1. Scan the product and enter how many you need. 2. The system plans the pick using FIFO (oldest first) — or FEFO (soonest-to-expire first) for medicine/feed/fluid/pooja — and shows you the exact slot(s) to take from before anything is finalised. 3. Fill in who is taking it, who authorised it, the on-duty Store Keeper, and a short reason (e.g. "morning feed for shed B"). A photo is required for liquids or weighed items. 4. Validate.
Why it matters This is the heart of the audit trail: every issue records who, why, and which keeper — so usage can be checked against the monthly cow-care plan.

Real trust example A helper needs 2 calcium bottles. The wizard says "take 2 from the December-expiry batch in slot PHARM01 / SH01 / C01" (FEFO). They enter taken-by, ordered-by, reason, validate — done, and it's all logged.
If stock is short The screen clearly warns "STOCK OUT" or "only N on hand" so you know to wait for a return or ask an Admin to receive more — it won't let you over-issue.

record.field: scan return, return, bring back, tool returned, returnable, restock

div.p: Scan Return is how you put stock back into the warehouse after it was taken out — for example a borrowed tool or a spare part that came back unused.

How it works It's the Scan Receipt screen with Return entry ticked. You scan the items coming back, choose the on-duty Store Keeper, and validate. The stock goes back onto a shelf and becomes available again.
Why it matters Returns keep your counts truthful. If a tool leaves and comes back but nobody records the return, the system thinks it's still out and may tell people it's unavailable.

Real trust example A helper borrowed a cordless drill (TOOL-DRILL-18V) for a fence repair. Job done, they bring it back and do a Scan Return. The drill is back on the shelf and the next person can issue it.

Important limit Returns are only for returnable items (tools, spares). Things that get used up — fluids, consumables, single-use items — cannot be returned; the system blocks it. If such an item is damaged, use the Damage workflow instead.

record.field: putaway, put away, slot assignment, auto-assign, where to store, clustering

div.p: Putaway is deciding which slot newly received stock goes into. You can scan the slot yourself, or let the system auto-pick a sensible spot when you validate a Scan Receipt.

How the system auto-picks (in order): 1. A slot/floor that already holds this same product (keep like with like). 2. An empty rack slot. 3. An empty floor area. 4. As a last resort, any slot (with a warning that products will mix).

Why it matters Good putaway keeps each product together so it's quick to find and count, and stops the same item being scattered across ten random slots. Auto-putaway also means a brand-new helper doesn't need to memorise the whole layout — just scan and validate.

Real trust example More calcium arrives. Because there's already calcium in PHARM01 / SH01 / C01, putaway sends the new bottles to that same slot, clustering the stock instead of opening a fresh, half-empty slot elsewhere.
Tip If you want it somewhere specific, just scan that slot's barcode during the receipt and the system uses your choice.

record.field: audit trail, history, who took it, accountability, immutable, traceability, log

div.p: The audit trail is the permanent record of who did what, when, and why with the trust's stock. Nothing important happens without a name attached.

ul.li: Scan Issue: who took it, who authorised it, the on-duty Store Keeper, the reason, and (for liquids/weighed items) a photo.
Scan Receipt / Return: who delivered it and which keeper received it.
Damage & Repair: who reported it, who authorised it, and the keeper on duty.

div.p: Why it matters The trust runs on donations and trust. Being able to show exactly where every bottle of medicine and sack of feed went — and on whose say-so — protects the helpers and the organisation. It also helps spot patterns, like one team over-pulling soap.

Real trust example Three months later someone asks where 10 litres of ghee went. The Admin opens the issue history and sees: taken by Ramesh, authorised by the cow-care lead, keeper on duty Suresh, reason "Janmashtami pooja", with a photo. Question answered in seconds.
Cannot be edited Once a stock-moving action is done, its record stays. Submitted inventory audits in particular are immutable — see the Inventory Audit and Cycle Count articles.

record.field: storekeeper, store keeper, roster, on duty, role, keeper, who is on the desk

div.p: A Store Keeper is a person who runs the store — receiving deliveries, issuing items, filing damage, and counting stock.

The trust keeps a roster of Store Keepers (their names live under Configuration → Store Keepers). On every Scan Issue, Receipt, Damage, or Repair, you pick the on-duty Store Keeper — the actual human at the desk right now.

Why it matters Many helpers are temporary or share one tablet, so the login alone doesn't tell you who physically handled the stock. Choosing the on-duty keeper makes the audit trail point to a real person.

Real trust example The shed tablet is signed in under a shared desk account. When Suresh issues feed in the morning, he picks "Suresh" from the roster. When Ramesh takes over after lunch, he picks "Ramesh". The history correctly shows who was on duty for each action.

Roles and permissions A Store Keeper can be given their own login with specific abilities (Scan Receive, Scan Issue, File Damage, Submit Audit). The other role is WMS Manager (Admin), who reviews audits, creates repair orders, sets up racks, and manages products. To retire a keeper, the Admin un-ticks "On the roster" — old records that mention them are kept.

record.field: damage, broken, expired, contaminated, scrap, damage location, write off

div.p: A Damage record is how you report stock that's broken, expired, contaminated, or otherwise no longer usable. Filing it moves that stock out of normal storage into a separate Damage area so nobody issues it by mistake.

How it works 1. Pick the product, quantity, source slot, and a reason (Broken / Expired / Contaminated / Other — "Other" needs a note). 2. Fill in who reported it, who authorised it, and the on-duty keeper. 3. Confirm. The stock moves to the Damage location and the event is logged.
The form also gives a plain-English recommendation — repair it, buy a replacement urgently, or just note it — based on whether the item is repairable and how much is left elsewhere.

Why it matters Broken or expired items sitting on the shelf cause wrong counts and dangerous mistakes (issuing expired medicine!). Recording damage keeps usable stock clean and creates an honest record.

Real trust example A helper finds a cracked bottle of calcium. They file a Damage (reason: Broken), and it's moved off the shelf. If that was the trust's last unit of a tool, the system flags an urgent buy and pings the Managers.

record.field: repair, repair order, fix, in repair, technician, scrap, returnable tool

div.p: A Repair Order tracks a damaged-but-fixable item through getting mended and coming back into service. It's used for returnable things like tools and equipment.

ul.li: Draft → the order is created (often straight from a Damage record).
In repair → the item is sent to the Repair area and is in the technician's hands.
Done → it's fixed and returned to a slot, ready to issue again.
Scrapped → it couldn't be fixed and is written off.

div.p: Each step records who reported it, who authorised it, and the keeper on duty.
Why it matters Good tools are expensive for a donation-funded trust. Repairing and returning them — instead of buying new — saves money, and tracking it means a broken tool never just "disappears".

Real trust example The cordless drill's battery fails. A helper files Damage, then clicks Create Repair Order. It goes "In repair", a technician replaces the battery, and it's marked Done — back in its slot and issuable again. If the drill were beyond saving, it would be Scrapped instead.

record.field: cycle count, inventory audit, recount, stocktake, variance, count due, 30 days

div.p: A cycle count is checking that what's physically on a shelf matches what the system says — done slot by slot, a little at a time, instead of one giant yearly stocktake.
The system flags any slot that hasn't been counted in over 30 days on the Cycle Count Due list and reminds Managers weekly.

The Inventory Audit (the structured walk) An Admin creates an audit and assigns a Store Keeper. The keeper walks the racks, scans, and enters the counted quantity next to the system's expected quantity. Differences ("variances") are highlighted. The keeper submits; the Admin then accepts (the system adjusts the books to match the count) or rejects (the keeper re-walks it).
Why it matters Counts drift over time — a missed return, a hand-grab nobody logged. Regular counting keeps the numbers trustworthy so issues and orders are based on reality.

Real trust example The feed-store slot hasn't been counted in 40 days, so it appears on Cycle Count Due. During the audit the keeper counts 18 sacks but the system expected 20. On accept, the books drop to 18 and the trail records who counted and who approved.
Cannot be rewritten Once an audit is submitted, its count lines are locked — they can't be quietly edited or deleted. To change anything, the Admin rejects it and the keeper does a fresh walk.

record.field: backup, encrypted, dump, gpg, data safety, disaster recovery, restore

div.p: A backup is a complete, encrypted copy of the warehouse system's data, saved so everything can be recovered if the main computer fails, is lost, or gets corrupted.

Backups are written as encrypted files (.dump.gpg) on a schedule, and each one's size, checksum, and result are recorded in the Backup & DR Audit dashboard. No passwords or secrets are ever stored in that record — only filenames, sizes, and status.

Why it matters All the trust's stock history — every receipt, issue, audit, and the location map — lives in one database. If that's lost without a backup, years of records vanish. Backups are the safety net.

Real trust example The store-room PC's drive dies one morning. Because an encrypted backup ran the previous afternoon, an Admin restores it onto a new machine and the trust is back to within a day of where it was — all the medicine and feed history intact.

Important A backup is only trustworthy if it has been proven to restore — which is exactly why we run a weekly Restore drill (see that article). The system also raises a warning if no successful backup has been recorded in the last 24 hours.

record.field: restore drill, disaster recovery, dr, test restore, weekly, pg_restore, verify backup

div.p: A restore drill is a weekly practice run that proves the latest backup can actually be recovered — without ever touching the live system.

The drill decrypts the newest backup, checks it's complete and structurally sound, and (in a full run) restores it into a temporary throwaway database that's deleted afterwards. The result is logged to the Backup & DR Audit dashboard.

Why it matters "A backup that has never been restored is not a backup." A backup file can look fine but be silently broken — cut off mid-write, hit by a software change, or locked by a changed password. A weekly drill catches all three within 7 days, before a real emergency.

Real trust example The backup password was rotated but nobody tested it. The next weekly drill fails to decrypt and immediately flags the problem — so it's fixed while the data is still safe, instead of being discovered during an actual disaster when it's too late.
Health link If no successful drill has run in over 7 days, the system marks backup health as DEGRADED and notifies the Managers.

record.field: health check, /wms/health, monitoring, status, healthy degraded critical, uptime, endpoint

div.p: A health check is a quick automatic status report on whether the warehouse system is safe and running. The system answers at the web address /wms/health and returns one of three statuses:

ul.li: HEALTHY — recent backup and a recent restore drill. All good.
DEGRADED — something's slipping: the backup is over 24 hours old, or the restore drill is over 7 days old. Still running, but needs attention.
CRITICAL — no successful backup has ever been recorded, or the system can't be reached. Act now.

div.p: Why it matters Problems with backups are invisible until you need them. The health check turns "are we protected?" into a single glance, and a monitoring tool can poll it automatically and alert someone the moment status drops.

Real trust example A monitoring service checks /wms/health every few minutes. Yesterday's 4:30 PM backup didn't run, so the status turns DEGRADED and an alert goes out. The Admin fixes the backup the same morning — long before anyone needs to restore.
Safe to expose The health report deliberately contains no sensitive data — only statuses and how old the last backup/drill are — so it's safe for a monitor to read without a password.

record.field: Admin Path 1: What this system is and what it does
admin overview manager system wms purpose non-profit trust cow care

div.p: You will learn: what the warehouse system is for, and the big picture before the detailed lessons.

This is the Warehouse Management System (WMS) for the trust. The trust buys and uses things (cattle feed, medicine, ghee for pooja, tools, cleaning items). It never sells them. So there are no customer orders or prices to worry about — only receiving, storing, issuing, and keeping the count honest.

Steps to get oriented: 1. Log in. As an Admin you are in the group WMS / Manager, which can see and do everything. 2. Open the WMS menu. You will see Operations (the daily scanning work), Configuration (racks, slots, store-keeper roster, carton barcodes), and Reporting (live dashboards). 3. Open the Help Center and read the role lessons in order — this one is the start of your path. 4. Note the two everyday jobs the system protects: every stock move is scanned (not typed from memory) and every move records who did it (the audit trail).
Why it matters: A small, shared, volunteer-run store fails when people "update stock later" or nobody is accountable. This system makes the honest way the only easy way.

ul.li: Treating it like a shop with sales — there are no sales here.
Skipping the lessons and clicking around blind; the paths are short and ordered for a reason.
Doing daily scanning yourself as the only Admin — train Store Keepers so the work spreads.

record.field: Admin Path 2: How the warehouse is laid out (Rack, Compartment, Slot, Zone, Floor)
admin rack compartment slot zone floor shelf column grid location structure layout

div.p: You will learn: the five location types and how stock physically maps to them.

The layout has three levels plus two extra area types: 1. Rack — a real shelving unit, drawn as a grid of shelves (rows) x columns. The default is 6 shelves x 3 columns. 2. Compartment — a rectangle on that grid (for example shelves 1-3, column 1). It can be one square, tall, wide, or a block. 3. Slot — the actual spot that holds stock. A compartment has one or more slots. Stock always lives in a slot. 4. Zone — a building, floor, or area that groups several racks together. 5. Floor — open / pallet / yard storage where stock sits directly, with no compartment or slot underneath.
Important: "Shelf" and "Column" are just grid coordinates, not separate records. Only Rack, Compartment, Slot, Zone, and Floor are real locations in the system.

Steps to view it: 1. Go to WMS > Configuration to see racks, compartments, and slots. 2. Open a rack's grid heat-map to see, square by square, what is stored where. 3. Compare it to the real shed — the screen should match the shelves.
Why it matters: Because stock lives in a slot, the system can tell a keeper the exact square to walk to, and reports can show occupancy per rack.

ul.li: Thinking shelf/column are separate places to create — they are not.
Leaving stock "on the floor" with no Floor location defined for it.
Letting the screen and the real shed drift apart — fix mismatches the same day.

record.field: Admin Path 3: Creating and laying out racks, compartments and slots
admin rack generator create slot compartment grid labels constraints capacity barcode print

div.p: You will learn: how to build the storage map and print labels so the shed matches the screen.

Steps: 1. Go to WMS > Configuration > Racks (or use the Rack Generator wizard) to create a rack. Set its shelf count and column count (default 6 x 3). 2. Add compartments as rectangles on that grid (top/bottom shelf, left/right column). A compartment must sit inside its rack's grid — the system blocks one that spills over the edge. 3. Give each compartment one or more slots. One slot per compartment is fine to start. 4. Optionally set a capacity hint on a slot. This is a soft hint shown in the screen, not a hard limit. 5. Print labels: open Slots, select up to 100, then the menu Print > WMS Location Label. Stick each label where a hand can see it while reaching in. 6. Walk the floor with the rack grid open and confirm physical = software.
Why it matters: Every slot has its own barcode. Good labels are what make scanning fast and putaway error-free.

ul.li: Building a compartment bigger than its rack grid — the system will refuse it.
Forgetting that a compartment's parent must be a rack, and a slot's parent must be a compartment.
Printing labels but not sticking them, or sticking them where they cannot be seen.

record.field: Admin Path 4: Users, the two roles, and capability switches
admin users roles permissions store keeper manager capability groups repair tech buyer access

div.p: You will learn: the role model and how to give each helper exactly the access they need.
There are two main roles:

ul.li: WMS / Store Keeper — the everyday operator (scanning, damage, audits). Can read every report but cannot edit racks or products.
WMS / Manager — the Admin. Can do everything.

div.p: On top of Store Keeper there are capability switches you tick per person: 1. Scan Receipt + Scan Return 2. Scan Issue (outbound) 3. File damage events 4. Submit inventory audits 5. Manage carton aliases + labels

A Store Keeper with no switches can log in and look around, but the Scan and Damage menus stay hidden until you grant a switch. There are also optional sub-roles: Repair Tech (can start/finish/scrap repairs) and Buyer (sees forecasts, drafts purchase orders).

Steps: 1. Go to Settings > Users. Create one login per person, or one shared login per shift (the on-duty human is still recorded separately — see the audit lesson). 2. Add the user to WMS / Store Keeper. 3. Tick only the capability switches that person needs. 4. Grant Repair Tech or Buyer only when that job is actually theirs.
Why it matters: Least access prevents accidents. A keeper cannot reach Odoo's raw Inventory app — the WMS scan flows are deliberately the only way they move stock.

ul.li: Making everyone a Manager "to save time" — that removes every guardrail.
Forgetting to tick a capability and then wondering why a menu is missing.
Granting Repair Tech or Buyer to people who do not do those jobs.

record.field: Admin Path 5: How stock flows in and out (FIFO and FEFO)
admin stock flow fifo fefo expiry in_date receipt issue return removal oldest earliest

div.p: You will learn: the in-and-out flow and the two rules the system uses to pick which stock leaves first.
The flow: stock comes in via Scan Receipt, sits in a slot or floor zone, and leaves via Scan Issue. Returns of reusable items come back via Scan Return.

FIFO — First In, First Out: the stock that arrived earliest leaves first. The system stamps an arrival time (in_date) on every receipt and, when you issue, automatically picks the oldest first across all slots. The keeper never has to remember which sack is oldest.

FEFO — First Expiry, First Out: for things that spoil, arrival order is not enough. For the kinds medicine, feed, fluid, and pooja (and anything with an expiry date set), the system switches to picking the soonest-to-expire batch first. So a new medicine batch expiring in 2027 is never handed out while an older one expiring next month still sits on the shelf.

Steps to confirm it works: 1. Open Reporting > Oldest Stock First (FIFO) and check the aging buckets. 2. Open the Expiry Alert report to see what is close to expiry. 3. Set an Expiry date on perishable products so FEFO and the alert can do their job.
Why it matters: FIFO stops old stock rotting forgotten at the back; FEFO stops the trust handing out a medicine or feed that expires first while keeping a fresher one.

ul.li: Leaving expiry dates blank on medicine/feed/fluid/pooja — FEFO then has nothing to sort by.
Telling a keeper to "grab any one" — let the scan plan choose for them.
Assuming FIFO covers perishables; for those kinds, FEFO is the rule.

record.field: Admin Path 6: The audit trail, the roster, and immutable audits
admin audit trail roster storekeeper immutable chatter taken by ordered by accountability who did it

div.p: You will learn: how the system records who did every stock move, and why submitted audits cannot be changed.
Every action that moves stock records an audit set:

ul.li: Who physically handled it (taken by / reported by / delivered by)
Who approved it (ordered by / authorised by)
Who was on the desk — picked from the Store Keeper roster

div.p: These are saved on the resulting record and written into the chatter (the message log at the bottom of every record). If a login is shared across a shift, the system also records the logged-in account automatically — so you know both which human and which session.

Steps: 1. Go to WMS > Configuration > Store Keepers and add one row per real person (Lakshmi, Ramesh, Suresh...). Wizards make keepers pick a name from this roster. 2. To review history, open any picking, damage, or repair record and read the chatter. 3. For a structured count, use Inventory Audits: you create an audit and assign a keeper, the keeper walks and counts, then Submits. You Accept (the system applies the corrections) or Reject (the keeper re-walks).

Why it matters: A submitted audit is the count of record. Its lines are locked — they cannot be deleted or quietly rewritten, even by an Admin or a script. To change a wrong count you reject the audit and a fresh one is walked. This is what makes the trail trustworthy.

ul.li: Leaving the roster empty so keepers cannot name themselves.
Trying to "fix" a submitted audit by editing lines — reject and re-walk instead.
Ignoring the chatter; it is your free, automatic history of who did what.

record.field: Admin Path 7: Backups and the weekly restore drill
admin backup restore drill encrypted dump gpg passphrase disaster recovery DR off-site weekly

div.p: You will learn: how the trust's data is protected and why a backup is only real once it has been restored.

The system makes encrypted backups (an encrypted .dump.gpg file) on a schedule. But a backup that has never been restored is not a backup — so a restore drill runs weekly to prove the latest backup can actually be recovered, without ever touching the live database.

Steps to keep this healthy: 1. Make sure a daily backup task is scheduled (Windows Task Scheduler, every afternoon at 4:30 PM). 2. Set a real backup passphrase in the .env file — the drill refuses to run while it is still the placeholder. 3. Let the weekly drill run (Sunday early morning). It checks the backup is complete and decryptable. Once a quarter, run a full restore drill so the database actually rebuilds into a throwaway copy. 4. Keep an off-site copy of the encrypted backups (a NAS or cloud) and drill against it at least monthly.

Why it matters: Three silent failures — a half-written backup, a schema change that breaks restore, and a rotated-but-untested passphrase — are caught only by an end-to-end restore. The weekly drill catches all three within seven days.

ul.li: Leaving the passphrase as the default placeholder.
Keeping the only backup on the same machine as the live system.
Assuming backups work — never restoring is the classic way to lose everything.

record.field: Admin Path 8: Watching system health (/wms/health and the DR dashboard)
admin health observability monitoring heartbeat backup audit dashboard healthy degraded critical endpoint

div.p: You will learn: the two ways to see at a glance whether the system is well.

1. The health endpoint. Visiting /wms/health returns a small status report: whether the database is reachable, how many hours since the last backup, how many days since the last restore drill, and any warnings. The overall status is one of:

ul.li: HEALTHY — all good.
DEGRADED — working, but something needs attention (for example a backup is overdue).
CRITICAL — a serious problem; needs action now.

div.p: The page is safe to open or to point a monitoring tool at — it deliberately shows only ages and a status, never filenames, paths, or secrets.
2. The Backup & DR Audit dashboard inside the WMS shows the same backup and drill heartbeats in a friendly screen.

Steps: 1. Bookmark /wms/health and glance at it daily, or have a monitor poll it. 2. If it shows DEGRADED or CRITICAL, open the Backup & DR Audit dashboard to see which heartbeat is stale. 3. Act on the warning (usually: a backup or drill did not run — check Task Scheduler).
Why it matters: Problems with backups and recovery are invisible until you need them. A status you check every day turns an invisible risk into an obvious to-do.

ul.li: Never looking at the health status until something has already broken.
Ignoring DEGRADED because "it still works" — that is the warning before CRITICAL.
Exposing the system to the internet without reading the security lesson first.

record.field: Admin Path 9: Reading the reports and dashboards
admin reports dashboards stock oldest occupancy reorder dead slow expiry forecast monthly consumption

div.p: You will learn: which dashboard answers which question. All reports are live views on the real stock — they never hold a stale copy.

Steps — open WMS > Reporting and learn these: 1. Current Stock by Product / by Slot — what we have and where. 2. Oldest Stock First (FIFO) — what has been sitting longest (aging buckets) so old stock is used before it rots. 3. Expiry Alert — perishables close to their expiry date. 4. Stock Movement History — every in/out move over a date range. 5. Low Stock / Reorder Suggestions — what is running low and roughly how much to buy (the buying figure is computed, not guessed). 6. Location Occupancy — how full each rack is. 7. Dead / Slow Stock — items barely moving, so the trust stops over-buying them. 8. Damaged Items and Repair Pipeline — open damage and repairs in progress. 9. Monthly Consumption — how much of each item the trust uses per month.
Why it matters: These dashboards turn raw stock numbers into decisions: what to buy, what to use first, what to stop buying, and where the gaps are.

ul.li: Exporting numbers into a separate spreadsheet and editing them — the dashboards are already live and correct.
Buying more of a Dead/Slow item out of habit.
Ignoring the Expiry Alert until items have already expired.

record.field: Admin Path 10: Overseeing damage and repair
admin damage repair recommendation urgent buy returnable scrap state machine notification manager

div.p: You will learn: how damage and repair work, and what the Admin must approve.
When a keeper files a Damage event and picks the product, the system shows a coloured recommendation banner:

ul.li: URGENT BUY (red) — a non-returnable item with no spare anywhere. Buy a replacement now.
Repair needed (yellow/blue) — a reusable item; consider opening a Repair Order.
Just a note (grey) — a non-returnable item but you still have spares; no action beyond recording it.

div.p: If the recommendation is URGENT BUY, every WMS Manager gets a notification in their Discuss inbox automatically.
Repair Orders follow a simple state machine: draft → in repair → done (or scrapped). Each step moves the item between the Damage and Repair locations and records the audit set.

Steps: 1. Watch your inbox for URGENT BUY notifications and act on them. 2. Open Operations > Repair Orders to start, finish, or scrap repairs (only Managers and Repair Techs can do this). 3. Use the Repair Pipeline report to see what is stuck in repair.
Why it matters: Damaged stock that is not recorded becomes a silent shortage. The recommendation engine tells you instantly whether a breakage is an emergency or just a note.

ul.li: Ignoring URGENT BUY notifications until the cows or pooja run out.
Cancelling a repair that is in repair — you must Finish or Scrap it first so stock is not orphaned at the Repair location.
Letting items sit forever in the repair pipeline.

record.field: admin troubleshooting scanner camera menu missing health critical backup drill mobile https fixes

div.p: You will learn: quick fixes for the problems you will most often be asked about.

Steps — match the symptom to the fix: 1. A keeper says a menu (Scan / Damage / Audit) is missing. They are missing the matching capability switch. Open their user and tick it (see the users lesson). 2. Scans land in the box but never process. The scanner is not sending an Enter key. Set the scanner to add a CR/LF (Enter) suffix (print the config barcode from its manual). 3. The camera will not open on a phone. Cameras only work over HTTPS (or on localhost). Use a Cloudflare tunnel to get HTTPS, or have the operator upload an existing photo instead. 4. Phone cannot reach the system over WiFi. Open port 8069 in Windows Firewall, and use the host PC's correct LAN IP. 5. /wms/health shows CRITICAL or DEGRADED. Open the Backup & DR Audit dashboard; usually a backup or drill did not run — check Windows Task Scheduler. 6. Restore drill failed. The most common cause is the passphrase still being the placeholder, or the backup file being truncated — re-run the backup and set a real passphrase.
Why it matters: Most "the system is broken" reports are small configuration issues. Knowing these six covers the large majority.

ul.li: Reinstalling or restoring when a one-tick capability or a scanner setting was the real fix.
Exposing the system on the internet without the security guardrails.
Letting a failed drill sit unfixed — that is the one failure that can lose all data.

record.field: Keeper Path 1: Getting started as a Store Keeper
keeper store keeper start login tablet beginner mode menu operations daily

div.p: You will learn: what your job is and how to find your way around on your first day.

As a Store Keeper you do the daily hands-on work: take in deliveries, put them away, hand things out, take reusable things back, and report damage. You do not edit racks or products — that is the Admin's job. You can look at every report.

Steps: 1. Log in (your supervisor gives you the login). On a tablet, the screen is touch-friendly. 2. Keep Beginner Mode ON at first — it shows extra hints and stronger "are you sure?" warnings. You can switch it off in your own preferences once you are confident. 3. Open the WMS > Operations menu. Your daily tools live here: Scan Receipt, Scan Issue (FIFO), Scan Return, and Damages. 4. If a menu you expect is missing, tell your Admin — they grant each tool with a tick. 5. Search the Help Center for any word you do not know (try "FIFO" or "compartment").
Why it matters: The trust's whole stock count depends on you scanning every move at the time it happens. Doing it right is more important than doing it fast.

ul.li: Turning Beginner Mode off on day one and missing the safety prompts.
Guessing instead of searching the Help Center.
Doing stock moves "in your head" and planning to record them later.

record.field: Keeper Path 2: Barcodes and your scanner
keeper barcode scanner product slot rack carton code128 ean usb bluetooth enter suffix

div.p: You will learn: the kinds of barcodes you will scan and how to make your scanner behave.

Barcodes you will meet: 1. Product barcode — on the item itself; tells the system what it is. 2. Carton / bulk barcode — one scan stands for many units (for example one scan = 24 units). Set up by the Admin. 3. Slot barcode — stuck on the shelf spot; tells the system where. 4. Rack barcode — identifies the whole rack.

Steps: 1. Pick up the scanner. Any USB, wireless, or Bluetooth scanner works like a keyboard — no setup needed. 2. Click into the scan box of a wizard so the cursor blinks there. 3. Pull the trigger on the barcode. The line appears by itself — you usually do not press a button. 4. The cursor stays in the box, so you can scan the next item straight away. 5. No scanner? You can type the barcode by hand into the same box.
Why it matters: Scanning the printed barcode means the human and the computer always agree on what the item is — far safer than picking from a list by memory.

ul.li: Scanning before clicking into the box (the scan goes nowhere).
If scans appear but never process, the scanner is not sending Enter — ask the Admin to set a CR/LF (Enter) suffix.
Scanning a slot barcode when you meant the product, or the reverse — check the line that appears.

record.field: Keeper Path 3: Receiving a delivery (Scan Receipt)
keeper receiving scan receipt delivery quality check qc grn audit validate print slot in_date

div.p: You will learn: how to take in a delivery correctly, every single time.

Steps: 1. When a delivery arrives, count it at the door and do a quick quality check (visible damage, count matches, expiry on perishables). 2. Open WMS > Operations > Scan Receipt. 3. Scan each product or carton barcode. A line is added with a quantity (a carton fills in its unit count automatically). 4. Optionally scan the slot barcode to say where it will go; if you do not, the system suggests a slot for you. 5. Tick Quality check passed and fill the audit panel: the Store Keeper on duty (pick your name from the list) and who delivered it. These are required. 6. Press Validate & Print. The system records the stock into the slot, stamps the arrival time, and can print labels. 7. Walk to the slot, place the stock, and confirm the label matches.

Why it matters: The system refuses to finish until the quality check is ticked and your name is filled. This keeps a clean record of who received what, and stamps the arrival time that FIFO later uses.

ul.li: Placing stock on the shelf before scanning it in — never do this; scan first.
Forgetting to tick "Quality check passed" — Validate will stop you.
Silently throwing away damaged or short-shipped items — send them through the Damage flow instead.
Doing one big receipt for several separate deliveries — one entry per delivery.

record.field: Keeper Path 4: Putaway and finding the right slot
keeper putaway slot find auto assign cluster empty rack floor zone label match place stock

div.p: You will learn: where to place stock after receiving, and how the system helps you choose.

When you receive without scanning a slot, the system suggests one in this order: 1. A slot that already holds this same product (keep like with like). 2. Any empty rack slot. 3. Any empty floor zone. 4. A rack slot that already has something else (with a warning that you would be mixing products). 5. Any floor zone.

Steps: 1. Read the slot the wizard assigned (or scan the slot you want to use). 2. Walk to that exact slot — the label on the shelf matches the name on screen. 3. Place the stock and check the label one more time. 4. If the suggested slot is physically full or wrong, scan a different empty slot instead.
Why it matters: Keeping one product together in one place makes both picking and counting far easier, and avoids the confusion of two different items sharing a square.

ul.li: Ignoring the suggestion and dumping stock in the nearest gap.
Mixing two different products in one slot when an empty slot was available.
Placing stock in a slot whose label does not match what the screen says.

record.field: Keeper Path 5: Issuing stock the FIFO way (Scan Issue)
keeper issue scan issue fifo fefo oldest expiry plan validate photo short shortage audit taken by

div.p: You will learn: how to hand out stock so the oldest (or soonest-to-expire) goes first, automatically.

Steps: 1. Open WMS > Operations > Scan Issue (FIFO). 2. Scan the product and enter how many are needed. 3. The system builds a plan showing exactly which slots to take from — oldest first (FIFO). For medicine, feed, fluid, and pooja items it picks the soonest-to-expire first (FEFO). You do not have to decide which batch. 4. Fill the audit panel: who is taking it, who ordered/approved it, and the on-duty Store Keeper. 5. If the product is measured (litres, kg), you must attach a photo of the dispensed amount before you can finish. 6. Press Validate. The stock leaves and the move is recorded with your audit details.

Why it matters: You do not have to remember which sack is oldest — the plan tells you. This stops old stock rotting at the back and stops a soon-to-expire medicine sitting while a fresher one is handed out.

ul.li: Picking from a different slot than the plan shows "because it is closer" — that breaks FIFO/FEFO.
Skipping the required photo for measured items (Validate will stop you).
If the system says short (not enough stock), do not part-issue and hope — tell the Admin so it can be bought.
Taking material first and planning to log it later — always scan at the moment you hand it out.

record.field: Keeper Path 6: Taking reusable items back (Scan Return)
keeper return scan return returnable tool spare reusable consumable fluid refuse slot

div.p: You will learn: how to put a reusable item back into stock, and which items can never come back.

Some things survive use and can return to the shelf: tools, spares, raw materials, cloth, safety gear. Other things cannot — once they leave they are spent, contaminated, or impossible to reseal: feed, medicine, fluids, ghee/pooja items, cement, soap.

Steps: 1. Open WMS > Operations > Scan Return. 2. Scan the item coming back. 3. Fill the audit panel (who is returning it, who is on duty). 4. Choose or scan the slot it goes back to. 5. Press Validate. The item is added back into stock.
Why it matters: Returning a tool puts it back on the books so the next person can find it. But returning a consumable would create stock that does not really exist.

ul.li: Trying to return a non-returnable item (feed, medicine, fluid, pooja, cement...) — the wizard will refuse it and list which products are not returnable.
Returning a tool to the wrong slot, so the next person cannot find it.
Putting a returned item straight on the shelf without scanning it back in.

record.field: keeper damage damaged broken report recommendation urgent buy photo audit confirm slot quantity

div.p: You will learn: how to report something broken, expired, or unusable — and what the colours mean.

Steps: 1. Open WMS > Operations > Damages > New. 2. Pick the product, the slot it is in, and how many are damaged. 3. Say who reported it and fill the rest of the audit details. 4. Read the coloured banner the system shows:

ul.li: Red (URGENT BUY) — there is no spare anywhere; a Manager is alerted to buy a replacement.
Yellow/Blue (repair) — the item can be repaired; a Repair Order may be opened.
Grey (just a note) — you still have spares; you are only recording it.

div.p: 5. Add a photo if you can — it helps the Admin decide. 6. Press Confirm. The damaged stock is moved out of its slot into the Damage area, with your name on the record.
Why it matters: Damage that is reported keeps the count honest and warns the Admin before the trust runs out of something important (like feed or medicine).

ul.li: Quietly throwing damaged stock away — the count then shows items that are gone.
Entering more than is actually in the slot — the system will block a quantity bigger than what is there.
Leaving an audit field blank — Confirm will stop you until who-reported-it is filled.

record.field: Keeper Path 8: What happens with repairs
keeper repair create repair order view read only repair tech linked back link state

div.p: You will learn: your part in the repair process, and where it stops.
When you file a damage on a reusable item, you may see a Create Repair Order button on the damage form. Clicking it opens a repair request, already filled in from your damage report.

Steps: 1. On a confirmed damage of a repairable item, click Create Repair Order if your supervisor wants it repaired. 2. That creates the repair request and links it back to your damage event (the Linked repair order field). 3. You can open and read that repair order, but you cannot change it. The buttons to Start, Finish, or Scrap the repair are hidden from you. 4. A Repair Tech or the Admin does the actual repair steps from the Repair Orders menu.
Why it matters: You raise the request; the repair itself is handled by someone with the Repair Tech role. This keeps a clear hand-off and avoids stock getting stuck halfway through a repair.

ul.li: Expecting to finish a repair yourself — that is the Repair Tech's job.
Clicking Create Repair Order for an item that just needs a note (the grey banner) — only open a repair when the item is worth repairing.
Losing track of the linked repair — follow the back-link on your damage event.

record.field: Keeper Path 9: Stock counts and inventory audits
keeper stock adjustment cycle count audit walk count variance submit immutable roster reject

div.p: You will learn: how to count stock honestly and hand a count to the Admin.
There are two counting jobs:

ul.li: Cycle count — a quick recount of a few slots, comparing the shelf to the screen.
Inventory audit — a structured walk the Admin assigns to you.

div.p: Steps for an audit: 1. The Admin creates an audit and assigns it to you; it lists the slots and the expected quantity for each. 2. Walk to each slot, count what is really there, and type it in the Counted column. 3. The system shows the variance (what you counted minus what was expected) and highlights mismatches. 4. Pick your name as the on-duty Store Keeper. 5. Press Submit. The Admin is notified and reviews it.

Why it matters: Once you Submit, the audit is locked — the counts cannot be changed or deleted, by you or anyone. That is what makes the count trustworthy. If something was wrong, the Admin rejects it and you walk a fresh one.

ul.li: "Fixing" the count to match the screen instead of writing what you actually see — write the truth, even if it is a mismatch.
Submitting before you have counted every line.
Forgetting to pick your on-duty name (Submit will stop you).
Thinking you can edit it after submitting — you cannot; ask the Admin to reject it.

record.field: Keeper Path 10: Your daily routine and common mistakes
keeper daily routine checklist habit same day scan first golden rules end of day spot check

div.p: You will learn: a simple daily rhythm that keeps the whole system accurate.

Steps — a typical day: 1. Log in and glance at Operations for anything pending. 2. Receive every delivery the moment it arrives — count, quality check, Scan Receipt, then shelve it. 3. Issue items only through Scan Issue (FIFO) — follow the plan, oldest/soonest-expiry first. 4. Take back reusable items through Scan Return. 5. Report anything broken or expired through Damages straight away. 6. Do a small spot count of a few high-value slots (a quick cycle count). 7. At the end of the day, ask: does the screen match the shelves? If not, flag it.

ul.li: Scan first, shelve second. Stock never touches a shelf before it is scanned in.
Same day, every move. "I will log it later" is the number one way the count goes wrong.
Write the truth. If a count is off, record what you see and tell the Admin.

div.p: Why it matters: The system is only as accurate as the moves you scan. Small, consistent habits keep the count trustworthy for everyone — including the cows, the pooja, and the next keeper on shift.

ul.li: Batching up moves to "do at the end" — do each one as it happens.
Skipping the quality check or the photo because you are in a hurry.
Hiding a mismatch instead of reporting it.

record.field: Viewer Path 1: What a read-only viewer can and cannot do
readonly viewer view only safe look reports search audit no edit permissions auditor

div.p: You will learn: exactly what your view-only access lets you do, and why it is set up this way.

As a read-only viewer you can look at everything but change nothing. You can open reports, search stock, and read the history of who did what — but you cannot move stock, edit products, or change racks. The Scan and Damage menus do not appear for you.

Steps: 1. Log in. Your menus are limited on purpose — that is normal. 2. Open WMS > Reporting to see live stock and history. 3. Use the global search to find a product or slot. 4. Open any record and read its chatter (the history log at the bottom) to see who did what and when. 5. If you genuinely need to change something, ask an Admin — do not ask for edit rights you do not need.
Why it matters: View-only access lets auditors, supervisors, and helpers check the numbers without any risk of accidentally changing them. You can look freely, knowing you cannot break anything.

ul.li: Thinking something is broken because a menu is missing — view-only is meant to be limited.
Asking for full edit rights when you only need to look.
Trying to "correct" a number yourself — report it to an Admin instead.

record.field: readonly viewer reports dashboards stock oldest occupancy expiry movement filter group live

div.p: You will learn: which report answers which question, so you can find facts quickly.
All reports are live — they always show the real, current stock. Nothing here is an old copy.

Steps — open WMS > Reporting: 1. Current Stock by Product / by Slot — "What do we have, and where?" 2. Oldest Stock First (FIFO) — "What has been sitting longest?" 3. Expiry Alert — "What is about to expire?" 4. Stock Movement History — "What came in and went out, and when?" 5. Location Occupancy — "How full is each rack?" 6. Damaged Items / Repair Pipeline — "What is broken or being fixed?" 7. Use the filters (date range, product, rack) and grouping at the top of each report to narrow down.
Why it matters: You do not need anyone to prepare a report for you — the answer is already on screen and up to date. This makes spot-checks and audits fast.

ul.li: Copying numbers into your own spreadsheet and trusting that instead of the live report.
Forgetting to clear a filter, then thinking stock is missing when it is just hidden.
Reading an old printout when the live report has since changed.

record.field: Viewer Path 3: Searching for stock and finding where it is
readonly viewer search find product sku slot where is it location quantity on hand filter

div.p: You will learn: how to find any item and see exactly where and how much there is.

Steps: 1. Use the global search at the top. Type the product name or its SKU (the code like FEED-00042 or MED-00007). 2. Open the product. The form shows Total on hand and in how many slots the item is stored right now. 3. Click the Where is it? button to see the per-slot breakdown — which slot, and how much in each. 4. To browse by place instead, open the Current Stock by Slot report and filter by rack. 5. You can sort and filter, but you cannot change any numbers — that is expected.
Why it matters: Anyone can answer "do we have it, and where?" in seconds, without disturbing a keeper or touching the stock.

ul.li: Searching a half-remembered name when the SKU would find it instantly.
Reading a quantity from an old screen — reopen the record for the live figure.
Assuming an item is out of stock because you searched the wrong spelling.

record.field: Viewer Path 4: Seeing the audit trail (who did what)
readonly viewer audit trail chatter history who did what taken by ordered by storekeeper immutable transparency

div.p: You will learn: how to read the full history of any stock move — a powerful tool for auditors and supervisors.

Every stock move records an audit set: who physically handled it, who approved it, and which Store Keeper was on duty. All of this is written into the chatter — the message log at the bottom of every record.

Steps: 1. Open any receipt, issue, damage, or repair record. 2. Scroll to the chatter at the bottom. 3. Read the audit message — it names the people involved and the time, and if a shared login was used, it also names the account that was logged in. 4. For structured counts, open a submitted Inventory Audit to see expected vs counted quantities and any variances.
Why it matters: This gives you complete transparency for free. You can trace any change back to a person and a moment — exactly what an audit needs.

ul.li: Overlooking the chatter — it is the richest part of the record.
Expecting to edit or delete history — for non-admins it is immutable, and submitted audits are locked for everyone. That is by design.
Asking a keeper "who did this?" when the chatter already tells you.

record.field: readonly viewer safe habits do not edit report problems escalate log out shared tablet privacy

div.p: You will learn: simple habits so you get the most from view-only access without causing confusion.

Steps: 1. Look, do not change. Open, read, filter, and sort freely — none of that affects the data. 2. If you spot a wrong number or something odd, note the record and tell an Admin. Do not try to fix it yourself. 3. On a shared tablet, log out when you finish so the next person starts clean. 4. Trust the live reports over any printout or your own notes — the screen is always current. 5. If a menu or button is missing, that is your role working as intended — not a fault.
Why it matters: View-only access exists so people can check the trust's stock safely. Good habits keep your checks reliable and keep the shared screens tidy for everyone.

ul.li: Asking for more access than you need "just in case".
Sharing a problem as a rumour instead of pointing the Admin to the exact record.
Leaving a shared tablet logged in under your view, confusing the next user.

record.field: receive receiving scan receipt inbound delivery goods in qc quality check arrival new stock

div.p: What this is for Use Scan Receipt every time new stock arrives at the store room or cow shed: sacks of feed, boxes of medicine, tins of ghee, new tools. It tells the system what came in, puts it on a shelf, and records who took the delivery.

Step by step 1. On the top menu open WMS -> Operations -> Scan Receipt. 2. Your cursor sits in the Scan here box. Point the scanner at each item's barcode and pull the trigger. Each scan adds a line to the table. If a box has a carton barcode, the system fills in the unit count for you. 3. Type a count by hand if an item has no barcode label yet (ask the Admin to onboard it later). 4. Optionally scan a slot barcode to choose where it goes. If you skip this, the system picks a slot for you when you finish. 5. Pick your name in Store Keeper on duty (this is required). Type who handed the goods over in Delivered by. 6. Physically count and check the goods. Then tick Quality check passed. 7. Click Validate & Print.
Why this workflow exists The trust buys, it never sells, so a clean record of what came in is the only proof of where the money went. It also starts the FIFO clock so the oldest stock leaves first.

ul.li: Do not tick Quality check passed without actually counting. The system will block you if the box is unticked, but only your honesty checks the count.
Do not guess quantities. Wrong numbers here break every later report.

div.p: Best practice Receive the delivery the moment it lands, while the driver is still there. Keep the cursor in the Scan box and let the scanner do the typing.

Trust example A vendor drops 20 sacks of cattle feed. The keeper scans the carton label, sees 20 appear, ticks Quality check passed, picks his name, types the driver's name in Delivered by, and clicks Validate & Print.

record.field: How to create a rack (Create Rack)
rack create racks shelves columns compartments slots build generate storage layout grid

div.p: What this is for A rack is the physical shelving unit in the store room. Creating one in the system builds the whole grid at once: the rack, its shelves x columns of compartments, and the slots inside that actually hold stock. Only an Admin/Manager does this.

Step by step 1. Open WMS -> Configuration -> Create Rack. 2. Pick the Parent location (usually a Zone like 'Pharmacy', or the main warehouse stock location). 3. Type a Rack code such as R01 (keep two digits: R01, R02...). Add a Display name like 'Pharmacy bottles' if you like. 4. Set Shelves (default 6) and Columns (default 3). This makes a 6x3 grid of compartments. 5. Set Slots per compartment (default 1 means the compartment itself is the storage spot). 6. Click Generate. The system creates the rack, every compartment, every slot, and a printable barcode for each.
Why this workflow exists Doing this once builds dozens of correctly named, correctly barcoded slots in seconds instead of by hand. Names like R01 / SH01 / C01 / SL01 mean anyone can find a spot.

ul.li: Do not reuse a rack code that already exists under the same parent; the system will refuse.
Do not delete a rack later if it holds stock or has history. The system blocks deletion on purpose. Tick Archived instead.
Leave the Custom layout box alone unless you truly need an odd shape; the visual builder fills it for you.

div.p: Best practice Match the numbers to the real shelving: count the actual shelves and columns before you type. Keep one rack code per physical rack.

Trust example The trust buys a new 6-shelf medicine rack. The Admin opens Create Rack, picks the Pharmacy zone, types R05, leaves 6 shelves x 3 columns, and clicks Generate. Eighteen labelled slots are ready to print and stick on.

record.field: How to create zones and floor areas
zone zones floor area open storage pallet yard generate building floor groups organise move to zone

div.p: What this is for A Zone is a building, floor, or area (like '1st Floor' or 'Outside Yard') that holds racks and floor areas. A Floor area is open storage with no shelves: a pallet stack, a yard bay, a single slab. Both are Admin tasks.

Step by step (one zone with everything inside) 1. Open WMS -> Configuration -> Generate Zone. 2. Type a Zone name like '1st Floor'. 3. To add racks, set How many racks, the Rack prefix (R), and shelves/columns per rack. 4. To add open areas, set How many open floor zones and the Floor prefix (F). 5. Click Generate. The zone, racks, slots, and floor areas are all created together.
Step by step (just floor areas) 1. Open WMS -> Configuration -> Generate Floor Zones. 2. Pick the Parent area, set a prefix (F gives F-01, F-02...), a count, and a start number. 3. Click Generate.
Why this workflow exists Not everything fits on a rack. Feed sacks, drums, and pallets sit on the floor. Floor areas let you scan, issue with FIFO, and report on that stock exactly like a rack slot.

ul.li: Re-running with the same names is safe (it skips ones that already exist), so do not worry about duplicates.
Do not store loose stock 'somewhere' off-system; every spot needs a barcode.

div.p: Best practice Group racks into zones that match the real building, then use Configuration -> (Move racks/floors into a zone) if existing racks need tidying under a new zone.

Trust example The trust opens a second store room upstairs. The Admin runs Generate Zone, names it '1st Floor', asks for 10 racks and 4 floor areas, and clicks Generate. The whole upstairs is mapped in one click.

record.field: How to assign a product to a slot
assign slot location put stock place shelf where to store auto assign destination

div.p: What this is for Assigning a slot tells the system the exact shelf spot (or floor area) where an item physically sits. It happens during Scan Receipt, and you can also let the system choose for you.

Step by step (choosing the slot yourself) 1. Start a receipt: WMS -> Operations -> Scan Receipt. 2. Scan the product so it appears as a line. 3. Scan the slot barcode on the shelf. The system attaches that slot to the most recent line that still has no slot. 4. The feedback line confirms 'Slot ... assigned'.

Step by step (letting the system choose) 1. Scan products only and leave the slot empty. 2. When you click Validate & Print, the system auto-picks a slot in this order: a slot already holding the same product, then any empty rack slot, then any empty floor area, then any rack slot, then any floor area.
Why this workflow exists If nobody records the spot, the next person hunts the whole store room. A slot per item means the Where is product X? report can point straight to it.

ul.li: Do not put two very different products in one slot if you can avoid it; the auto-picker only mixes products as a last resort and warns you.
Do not invent a slot in your head. Scan the printed label so the names match.

div.p: Best practice Keep the same product in the same slot every time (clustering). It speeds up counting and FIFO picking.
Trust example The keeper receives calcium boluses, scans the box, then scans the shelf label R05/SH02/C01/SL01. Next month, anyone searching 'calcium' is sent to that exact spot.

record.field: How to do putaway (get stock onto the shelf)
putaway put away store shelving move stock to shelf after receipt slot placement

div.p: What this is for Putaway means physically placing what you just received onto the correct shelf or floor area, and making sure the system agrees with reality. In this system, putaway happens as part of Scan Receipt rather than as a separate screen.

Step by step 1. Finish a receipt (see the Scan Receipt guide). When you scan a slot barcode, or let the system auto-assign, the stock is recorded at that spot. 2. Carry each item to the slot named on the label, for example R02/SH03/C01/SL01. 3. Place it physically where the system says it is. 4. If you decide a different shelf is better, scan that slot barcode during the receipt so the record matches where you actually put it. 5. To confirm afterwards, open WMS -> Reports -> Where is product X? and check the slot shown matches the real shelf.

Why this workflow exists Receiving is only half the job. If the box says R02 but you drop it on R09, every future search and FIFO pick points to the wrong place. Putaway keeps the digital map and the real room identical.

ul.li: Do not pile new stock 'temporarily' in a corner and forget to record where it ended up.
Do not move stock between slots without telling the system; use Scan Receipt's slot scan or ask the Admin.

div.p: Best practice Put away immediately after receiving, one item at a time, scanning the slot as you place it. Heavy or liquid items go on lower shelves.

Trust example After receiving 12 tins of ghee, the keeper walks them to the pooja-supplies rack, scans the slot label as he sets them down, and the Where is product X? report instantly shows the right spot.

record.field: How to issue stock (Scan Issue, FIFO)
issue scan issue fifo fefo take out give out outbound use stock oldest first expiry photo reason taken by

div.p: What this is for Use Scan Issue whenever stock leaves the store for use: feed for the shed, medicine for a calf, ghee for pooja, a tool for a job. The system automatically takes the oldest stock first (FIFO), or the soonest-to-expire first (FEFO) for medicine, feed, fluids, and pooja items.

Step by step 1. Open WMS -> Operations -> Scan Issue (FIFO). 2. Set Requested Qty, then scan the product barcode. The system shows a plan of which slot(s) it will take from, before anything moves. 3. Check the plan rows. If a slot is actually empty, reduce that row. 4. Fill the audit panel (all required): Taken by (who is carrying it away), Ordered by (who authorised it), Store Keeper on duty (you), and a Reason / usage note (for example 'morning feed for shed B'). 5. If the item is measured by weight or volume (kg, litres), snap the required Item photo. 6. Click Validate.
Why this workflow exists It forces older stock out first so nothing rots at the back, and it records who took what and why, which is how a non-profit proves its inventory was used honestly.

ul.li: Do not partial-issue during a stock-out. If the store is short, the system refuses on purpose so you flag the Admin instead of half-filling.
Do not leave the Reason blank or pick a name that is not really on duty.
A measured item will not validate without a photo.

div.p: Best practice Issue at the moment of handover, not later from memory. Trust the plan; the system already knows the oldest batch.

Trust example The keeper needs 5 calcium boluses. He scans them; FEFO plans them from the batch expiring this December, not next June. He types Taken by 'Dr Rao', Ordered by 'Farm lead', reason 'vaccination round for calves', and clicks Validate.

record.field: return returns scan return bring back tool spare borrowed returnable not returnable

div.p: What this is for Use Scan Return when something that left the store comes back unused and reusable: a tool borrowed for a job, a spare part not needed, raw material brought back. It puts the stock back on the shelf.

Step by step 1. Open WMS -> Operations -> Scan Return. (This is the same screen as Scan Receipt, already set to Return entry.) 2. Scan each returning item so it appears as a line. 3. Optionally scan the slot it should go back to, or let the system auto-assign. 4. Pick your name in Store Keeper on duty and note who brought it back in Delivered by. 5. Tick Quality check passed after you confirm the item is in good condition. 6. Click Validate & Print.

Why this workflow exists Returned tools and spares are still trust property and should go back into stock, not vanish. Recording the return keeps counts honest and makes the item available to the next person.

ul.li: Some items cannot be returned. Fluids and consumables are flagged not-returnable, and the system will refuse them at Validate, listing which ones. Those go through the Damage workflow if spoiled, not Return.
Do not return a broken item as if it were fine; if it is damaged, file a Damage instead.

div.p: Best practice Inspect before ticking Quality check passed. If an item comes back damaged, stop and use the Damages workflow.

Trust example A plumber borrowed a pipe wrench from the tools rack and brings it back clean. The keeper opens Scan Return, scans the wrench, scans its slot, ticks Quality check passed, and validates. The wrench is back in stock for the next job.

record.field: damage damaged broken expired contaminated spoiled scrap damage event report recommendation urgent buy

div.p: What this is for File a Damage when stock is broken, expired, contaminated, or otherwise no longer usable. It moves the bad stock out of normal storage into a Damage holding location and tells the Admin what to do next.

Step by step 1. Open WMS -> Operations -> Damages, then click New. 2. Pick the Product, the Quantity, and the Slot (the shelf or floor area it sits in). 3. Choose a Reason: Broken, Expired, Contaminated, or Other. If you pick Other, you must type a note explaining it. 4. As soon as you pick the product, a coloured banner suggests what to do (for example a red URGENT BUY, or a blue 'Open a Repair Order'). 5. Fill the audit fields: Reported by, Authorised by, and Store Keeper on duty (all required). 6. Click Confirm.

Why this workflow exists Damaged stock must leave the usable count immediately, or the system thinks the trust has feed or medicine it cannot actually use. It also creates an honest paper trail for spoilage.

ul.li: You cannot file more units than are actually free in the slot; the system blocks over-counting and stock already reserved for an in-progress issue.
Do not skip the audit fields; Confirm is blocked until who-reported / who-authorised / which-keeper are filled.
Do not throw the item away physically before confirming the record.

div.p: Best practice File the damage the moment you spot it, and read the banner. If it says repair, follow the Repairs workflow; if it says URGENT BUY, the managers are notified automatically.

Trust example A keeper finds a leaking medicine bottle. He opens Damages -> New, picks the product and its slot, reason Contaminated, fills the three audit names, and clicks Confirm. The bottle moves to the Damage location and the report updates.

record.field: How to repair a damaged item (Repair Orders)
