repair repairs repair order fix tool start repair mark done scrap in repair return slot technician

div.p: What this is for A Repair Order tracks a fixable item (usually a returnable tool or spare) from the Damage area, through repair, and back onto its shelf, or to scrap if it cannot be saved. Managers run repairs; the Admin authorises each step.

Step by step 1. The easiest start: open the confirmed Damage event and click Create Repair Order. It pre-fills the product, quantity, original slot, return slot, and the audit names. (Or open WMS -> Operations -> Repair Orders -> New for a standalone one.) 2. Make sure Reported by, Authorised by, and Store Keeper on duty are filled. 3. Click Start Repair. The item moves from the Damage location to the Repair-Out bench (state becomes In repair). 4. When the fix is finished, set the Return slot if it differs from the original, then click Mark Done. The item goes back to its slot and is available to issue again. 5. If it cannot be fixed, click Scrap instead. It is written off from the Repair-Out location.

Why this workflow exists The trust keeps tools, not throwaways. Repairing and returning them saves money, and the order keeps the item's location honest at every step instead of leaving it 'somewhere being fixed'.

ul.li: An In repair order cannot be cancelled; you must either Mark Done or Scrap it, otherwise the unit is stuck at Repair-Out with no owner.
A Done or Scrapped order is final; open a new Damage if the item fails again.
Every step needs the audit names filled.

div.p: Best practice Always start repairs from the Damage event so the history links up. Set the return slot before Mark Done so the tool lands back where keepers expect it.

Trust example A water pump is filed as damaged. The Admin clicks Create Repair Order, then Start Repair. After the technician fixes it, the Admin clicks Mark Done and the pump returns to its tools slot, ready for the next job.

record.field: How to verify backups are healthy
backup verify download encrypted health check dashboard dr audit last backup age stale

div.p: What this is for Verifying backups means checking that the trust's data is being saved safely and could be brought back if the computer died. An Admin should glance at this weekly.

Step by step 1. Open the Backup & DR Audit dashboard from the WMS menu. Each row is a backup or restore-drill event with its time, size, and a success tick. 2. Check the newest Database backup row is from the last 24 hours and shows success. 3. Check there is a recent Restore drill row (within the last 7 days) marked verified. 4. Open a web browser to the address /wms/health on the server. It returns HEALTHY, DEGRADED, or CRITICAL, plus the age of the last backup and last drill. 5. To grab a copy by hand, use WMS -> Configuration -> Download encrypted backup. It downloads one encrypted file.
Why this workflow exists A backup nobody checks is not a backup. If a backup silently stopped working, this is how you catch it within a day instead of discovering it after a disaster.

ul.li: Do not assume green forever; check weekly. A DEGRADED or CRITICAL status means a backup is stale or a drill failed.
Do not share or email the downloaded encrypted file casually; it is the whole database.
The health page shows ages and status only, never secrets, so it is safe for a monitor to poll.

div.p: Best practice Make the weekly backup check part of the same routine as the weekly inventory audit. If status is not HEALTHY, read the Restore drill guide and the deployment doc.

Trust example Every Monday the Admin opens the Backup & DR Audit dashboard, sees yesterday afternoon's database backup ticked green and Sunday's restore drill verified, opens /wms/health to confirm HEALTHY, and moves on.

record.field: How to run the weekly restore drill
restore drill recovery test backup recoverable pg_restore powershell dry run quarterly full restore

div.p: What this is for A restore drill proves that the latest backup can actually be brought back, without ever touching the live database. It runs a saved backup into a throwaway copy and checks it is complete. An Admin oversees it; it normally runs automatically every week.

Step by step (cheap weekly check) 1. Open PowerShell on the server. 2. Run the drill script in the project's scripts folder: scripts\restore-drill.ps1. By default this is a dry run, it checks the backup's contents in seconds without rebuilding anything. 3. Read the result. Exit code 0 means the backup is recoverable. Other codes point to the exact problem (missing file, decrypt failed, truncated dump, and so on).

Step by step (full restore, once a quarter) 1. Run scripts\restore-drill.ps1 -DryRun:$false. 2. The script builds a temporary database named wms_drill_<date>, restores into it, checks the users table exists, then drops it again automatically.

Why this workflow exists Three silent failures, a cut-off backup file, a database change that breaks restore, or a changed password that was never tested, are caught only by an end-to-end restore. The weekly drill catches them within 7 days.

ul.li: This is the DRILL, not a real recovery. For a real recovery use scripts\restore-native.ps1, which writes into the live database, only after reading the deployment doc.
If the script says the passphrase is still the placeholder, set the real one in the .env file first.
Do not delete the backups folder.

div.p: Best practice Leave the automatic weekly task running, and once a quarter run a full restore by hand to be extra sure. Each drill writes a line to the Backup & DR Audit dashboard so you have a record.

Trust example On the first Sunday of the quarter the Admin runs the full drill. The script restores the newest backup into a temporary wms_drill database, confirms it is complete, drops it, and logs a green verified row. The trust now knows its data is genuinely safe.

record.field: reports warehouse map where is product oldest stock occupancy movement history dead stock find search

div.p: What this is for The Reports menu answers everyday questions without digging through stock by hand: where something is, what is oldest, what is running low, what is expiring, and who issued what. Everyone can read reports; only Admins change the underlying data.
Step by step 1. Open WMS -> Reports. 2. Pick the report that matches your question:

ul.li: Where is product X? to find the slot holding an item.
Warehouse Map for a visual picture of the racks.
Oldest stock (FIFO) to see what should leave first.
Slot occupancy to see how full each slot is.
Movement history to see every receipt, issue, damage, and repair.
Expiry alerts for batches nearing their expiry date.
Dead stock for items that have not moved in a long time.

div.p: 3. Use the filters and group-by at the top to narrow the list (for example group Movement history by Store Keeper).
Why this workflow exists Reports turn the raw stock records into plain answers a busy helper can act on, so people stop walking the whole store room to find one bottle.

ul.li: Reports are read-only views; you cannot fix a wrong number here. If something looks wrong, the cause is usually a missed receipt or issue, fix that workflow.
Do not panic at a stock-out figure before checking the Damage and Repair areas, the units may be held there.

div.p: Best practice Start your shift with Where is product X? for anything you will issue, and let the Admin watch Expiry alerts and Dead stock weekly.
Trust example A helper is asked for deworming medicine. Instead of hunting, he opens Where is product X?, types the name, and is sent straight to slot R05/SH02/C01/SL01.

record.field: How to do an inventory / cycle-count check
cycle count inventory check stock count audit reconcile adjustment count due recount slot

div.p: What this is for A cycle count is physically counting the stock in a slot and comparing it to what the system says, then fixing any difference. It keeps the records trustworthy. The system flags slots that have not been counted in over 30 days.

Step by step 1. Open WMS -> Reports -> Cycle Count Due to see which slots are overdue (counted more than 30 days ago). 2. Go to the slot and physically count the stock. 3. Open WMS -> Operations -> Cycle Count (Odoo's Inventory Adjustments) and find that slot. 4. If the count matches, mark it counted. If it differs, enter the real counted quantity so the system updates. 5. If you also keep a formal monthly record, file it under WMS -> Operations -> Inventory audits (this needs the audit capability). Note: once an audit is submitted it is locked and cannot be edited.
Why this workflow exists Receipts and issues are entered by people, and people miscount. Regular cycle counts catch small errors before they grow, so reports stay honest.

ul.li: Do not adjust a quantity to 'make the system happy' without actually counting; that hides the real problem.
Do not edit a submitted audit; submitted audits are immutable on purpose. Start a new count instead.
Avoid counting a slot mid-issue, finish or wait for any in-progress Scan Issue first.

div.p: Best practice Count a few overdue slots each week rather than the whole store at once. Each cycle count resets that slot's 30-day clock, so the overdue list stays short.

Trust example The Cycle Count Due list flags the feed floor area. The keeper counts 42 sacks but the system shows 45. He opens Cycle Count, enters 42, and the record now matches the shed. Three sacks of error are caught early.

record.field: How to handle low stock and reordering
low stock reorder buying recommendation shopping list reorder summary vendor out of stock replenish forecast

div.p: What this is for This workflow spots items running low so the trust buys more before it runs out, and groups what to buy into a simple shopping list by vendor. It is mainly an Admin task.

Step by step 1. Open WMS -> Reports -> Low stock alerts to see items below their safe level. 2. Open WMS -> Reports -> Reorder summary to see a buying list grouped by vendor, with how many of each to order. 3. For tools and spares, check Tool / Spare fleet; for items about to expire, check Expiry alerts. 4. Decide what to buy and place the order with the vendor outside the system (the trust buys, it does not sell). 5. When the goods arrive, record them with Scan Receipt so the counts go back up.

Why this workflow exists Running out of feed or medicine for the cows is the worst outcome. These reports give early warning and turn scattered shortages into one clear order, instead of buying in a panic.

ul.li: Do not ignore an URGENT BUY alert. When a damaged item leaves zero usable stock, the managers get a Discuss message and the buying report flags it Critical.
Do not order without checking the Damage and Repair areas first, some 'missing' units may just be out for repair.
Do not forget to Scan Receipt the new stock; until you do, the report still shows it as low.

div.p: Best practice Review Low stock alerts and Reorder summary on the same weekly cycle as cycle counts. Set sensible safe levels on the products so the alerts fire early enough to order calmly.

Trust example The Low stock alerts report shows cattle feed and mineral mix both low. The Admin opens Reorder summary, sees both come from the same vendor with a suggested quantity each, places one combined order, and Scan Receipts the delivery when it arrives.

record.field: Why can't I delete this slot (or rack)?
delete slot rack compartment blocked archive cannot remove location history

div.p: If you press Delete on a rack, compartment, slot, or floor area and the system stops you, that is on purpose. It is protecting your records.
The system blocks the delete for one of three reasons:

ul.li: It still has sub-locations. A rack holds compartments, which hold slots. Empty those first (slot, then compartment, then rack).
It still holds stock. Issue, scrap, or move the stock out first, then the slot becomes empty.
It has past movement history. Anything that has ever received or issued stock is part of the audit trail, and that trail must be kept forever.

div.p: What to do instead: archive it. On the location form, tick Archived (this sets it to inactive). The slot disappears from your day-to-day lists but every past record that mentions it stays safe.
Example: Slot R12 / SH01 / C01 / SL01 once held calcium bolus that was issued last month. Even though it looks empty now, deleting it would break the record of that issue. So you archive it instead.
Why it matters: the trust must be able to prove, months later, exactly where every item lived and who handled it. A deleted slot would leave a hole in that story.

record.field: reserved stock locked held cannot take in-flight issue available free quantity

div.p: Reserved means another job has already claimed those units, even though they are still sitting on the shelf.

Most often this happens because someone has a Scan Issue open and the system has planned to take those exact units. Until they press Validate (or cancel), those units are set aside so two people don't grab the same stock.
The number you can actually use is Free = On hand minus Reserved.
Example: Slot SH02 / C03 has 10 sacks of feed. Ramesh is half-way through issuing 4 of them. While his wizard is open, 4 are reserved, so only 6 are free for you right now.

ul.li: Wait a minute. Once the other person validates or cancels, the reservation clears.
If you only need what is free, reduce your quantity and carry on.
If a reservation seems stuck (the person walked away), ask the Admin to check the open issue.

div.p: Why it matters: reservations stop the warehouse from promising the same item to two people at once, which would push a slot count below zero.

record.field: blocked error red message cannot save validate confirm why stopped permission

div.p: When the system stops an action, it is almost always guarding your stock counts or your records. Read the red message first, it usually tells you exactly what to fix.
The most common reasons an action is blocked:

ul.li: A required field is empty. Issues, damage reports, and repairs need the audit details (who took it, who allowed it, which keeper is on duty) and a reason. Fill them in.
Not enough free stock. You asked for more than the slot has free (see Why is this stock reserved?).
A photo is required. Items measured by weight or volume (kg, litres) need a photo before you can validate.
A daily or per-issue limit was hit. Some items have a cap (see Why did my issue get blocked by a daily limit?).
You don't have permission. Some actions, like moving racks into a zone, are Admin-only.
The record is in the wrong state. For example, you can only scrap an item that is in repair.

div.p: What to do: read the message, fix the one thing it names, and try again. If it still won't go through and you don't understand why, stop and ask the Admin rather than working around it.
Why it matters: these blocks exist so a small mistake never turns into a wrong count that takes days to untangle.

record.field: Why must I record who took the stock?
taken by ordered by storekeeper reason usage note audit accountability who required

div.p: Every time stock leaves the store, the system asks for four things before it will let you finish:

ul.li: Taken by — the person physically carrying the items away.
Ordered by — the person who said it was OK to take them (Manager or cow-care lead).
Store Keeper on duty — you, the keeper running the desk right now, picked from the roster.
Reason / usage note — a short line saying why, e.g. "morning feed for shed B".

div.p: All four are required. The issue cannot go through without them.

Why it matters: the trust buys and uses everything itself, it never sells. The only way to know that feed, medicine, and ghee are being used properly, and not wasted or walking out the door, is to record who, who allowed it, and why, every single time.

Example: three months from now the Admin notices the soap stock dropped fast. Because every issue recorded a name and a reason, they can see it was used for a one-time deep clean of shed C, not lost. No name, no explanation, weeks of guessing.
This is also kind to you: an honest record protects you if anyone ever asks what happened to an item.

record.field: What do I do if I scan the wrong barcode?
wrong barcode mistake scan remove line delete undo correct mis-scan fix

div.p: Scanning the wrong item happens, and it is easy to fix as long as you catch it before you press Validate.

ul.li: In the Scan Receipt or Scan Issue wizard, find the wrong line in the list.
Remove it (click the small delete / X on that line).
Scan the correct barcode and carry on.

div.p: Nothing has moved yet at this stage, so removing a line costs you nothing.

Once you press Validate, real stock has moved and the record is part of the audit trail, so you cannot simply edit it. Tell the Admin. They will make an inventory adjustment (or a return) to put things right, and the correction is logged too.
If a scan does nothing at all: make sure the cursor is sitting in the scan box, tap it once if not, then scan again.
If a scan says "does not resolve to a product": the barcode isn't linked to anything yet. A vendor carton sticker may need a carton alias set up by the Admin, or the product label may need printing.
Why it matters: catching a mistake in the wizard is free; fixing it after validation needs an adjustment so the records stay honest.

record.field: What if two of us scan at the same time?
two people same time concurrent scan issue clash reserved conflict simultaneous keepers

div.p: It is safe for two keepers to work at the same time. The system is built to handle it.

When you plan a Scan Issue, the units you are about to take are reserved straight away. That means a second keeper planning an issue for the same product cannot grab the same units, they will only see what is still free.

Example: a slot has 10 bottles of dewormer. You plan to issue 7, so 7 become reserved. At the same moment Suresh scans the same dewormer, his wizard shows only 3 free. Nobody ends up with a slot count below zero.

ul.li: A smaller "free" number than you expected, because a colleague reserved some.
A short stock message telling you to reduce your quantity or wait.

div.p: What to do: if you are short because of someone else's open issue, either take the free amount now, or wait a moment for them to finish so the rest is released.

One more thing: if you open a record (like a damage report) right after another keeper saved it, you may see an orange banner saying "so-and-so saved this a few minutes ago". Read their changes before you save over them.
Why it matters: reservations and warnings let the whole team work at once without stepping on each other's counts.

record.field: Why did my issue get blocked by a daily limit?
daily limit cap blocked too much max per issue 24 hours rolling overuse exceeded

div.p: Some items have a built-in limit so they can't be over-pulled by mistake or habit. If you hit one, the system blocks the issue and tells you the numbers.
There are two kinds of limit, and an item may have either, both, or none:

ul.li: Max per issue — the most you can take in a single ticket. If you ask for more, split it or reduce the quantity.
Daily cap (24-hour rolling) — the most that can leave in any 24-hour window. The message shows how much already went out, what you're asking for, and the cap.

div.p: The 24-hour window is rolling, not a calendar day. It looks back exactly 24 hours from right now, so waiting a while may free up room as older issues age out.

Example: a strong medicine has a daily cap of 5. If 4 already went out in the last 24 hours and you try to issue 2, the total (6) is over 5, so it's blocked. Wait for the window to clear, or take 1 now.

ul.li: Reduce the quantity, or wait for the rolling window to clear.
If the cap is genuinely too low for real work, ask the Admin to raise it on the product (these limits live on the product's WMS Classification settings).

div.p: Why it matters: caps quietly protect costly or sensitive items, like medicine, from being drained faster than they should be.

record.field: beginner mode hints guidance new helper preferences turn off confirmations training easy

div.p: Beginner Mode is a helper setting that gives you extra on-screen guidance and stronger "are you sure?" confirmations while you learn the system.
It is on by default for everyone, so a brand-new helper is guided from their very first login. You can turn it off yourself once you feel confident, and turn it back on any time.
1. Click your name in the top-right corner. 2. Open Preferences. 3. Find the Warehouse (WMS) section and tick or untick WMS Beginner Mode.
You don't need Admin rights, this is your own personal setting and only affects what you see.
What it does for you: shows friendly hints next to fields, and asks for an extra confirmation before risky actions (like scrapping an item) so you don't do something final by accident.
Example: with Beginner Mode on, the first time you scrap something the system pauses to make sure you really mean it, because scrapping can't be undone.
Why it matters: new helpers, including temporary ones, can start work safely on day one without memorising everything first. Experienced keepers can switch it off for a faster screen.

record.field: Why can't I change an audit after I submit it?
audit submit locked immutable edit change line cannot delete count reject re-walk

div.p: Once you press Submit on an inventory audit, the count lines lock and you can no longer edit or delete them. This is on purpose.
A submitted audit is the official record of what you counted on the shelves that day. If anyone could quietly change it afterwards, the count would no longer be trustworthy.

If you spot a mistake after submitting: don't try to force a change. Instead, tell the Admin. They can reject the audit, which sends it back so a fresh audit can be walked. The keeper then re-counts the flagged slots and submits again.

p.b: The audit flow in plain steps:

div.p: 1. Admin creates an audit and assigns a keeper. 2. Keeper presses Start, walks the racks, and types in the counted quantity for each line. 3. Keeper presses Submit (the Admin is notified automatically). 4. Admin either Accepts (the system adjusts the books to match your count) or Rejects (re-walk needed).
Example: you submit, then realise you counted slot C02 in a hurry. You can't edit it now, so the Admin rejects the audit and you re-walk just to be sure. The honest record stays intact.
Why it matters: trust in the stock figures is built by counting carefully and never editing the count after the fact.

record.field: Why does it say STOCK OUT or that I'm short?
stock out short shortfall not enough cannot issue empty warehouse return receipt

div.p: When you plan a Scan Issue, the system checks every slot in the warehouse for that product. If it can't find enough, it tells you straight away rather than letting a bad issue go through.

ul.li: STOCK OUT — there is none of this product anywhere in the warehouse. The issue can't proceed.
Short by X — there is some, but less than you asked for. It shows how much is on hand and how much you're missing.
Reduce the quantity to what is actually available and issue that.
Wait for stock to come back through Scan Return (for items that can be returned).
Ask the Admin to receive more via Scan Receipt if a delivery has arrived but isn't entered yet.

div.p: You cannot validate while you are still short, this stops the slot count going negative.
Example: you ask for 20 bags of lime but only 12 are on hand. The wizard shows "12 on hand, 8 short". Issue 12 now and ask the Admin when the next delivery lands.
Why it matters: the system would rather tell you the truth now than create a record claiming you issued stock that was never there.

record.field: SAFETY: Never delete a location with history, archive it
safety delete location archive history audit warning never remove rack slot inactive

div.p: Warning: deleting the wrong thing can erase records you can never get back. When in doubt, archive, don't delete.

Racks, compartments, slots, and floor areas often carry a long history of receipts and issues. That history is the trust's proof of where everything has been. The system will block a delete that would break it, but please don't go looking for ways around the block.

ul.li: A slot or rack you no longer use? Open its form and tick Archived (set it inactive).
It vanishes from your everyday lists, but every past record stays whole.
Only ever fully remove a location that has never held stock and never appeared in a movement, for example one you created by mistake a moment ago.

div.p: Example: an old rack in the corner is being retired. Don't delete it, archive it. Next year, if anyone asks what used to be stored there, the answer is still in the system.
If you're unsure, stop and ask the Admin. A deleted record can't be brought back; an archived one can be switched back on in seconds.
Why it matters: the trust must be able to account for every item, every donation, and every use, for a long time. Records are not clutter, they are the whole point.

record.field: SAFETY: Double-check expiry on medicine and feed (FEFO)
safety FEFO expiry medicine feed fluid pooja earliest first check date expired batch

div.p: Warning: giving out expired medicine or feed can harm the cows. Always take a moment to check the expiry date with your own eyes.

For medicine, feed, fluids, and pooja items, the system uses FEFO — First Expiry, First Out. When you issue, it automatically picks the batch that expires soonest, not just the oldest by arrival date. It will even pull from a different batch of the same item if that batch expires earlier.

ul.li: Read the slot the wizard tells you to pick from, and take from exactly that slot. The plan lists the right batch for a reason.
Check the expiry date printed on the item before it leaves your hands. If it has already passed, do not issue it.
An expired item should go through the Damage flow (reason: Expired), not out to the cows.

div.p: Example: you scan a calcium bolus. The wizard says take from the slot holding the batch expiring this December, not the fresh one expiring next year. That is FEFO doing its job, follow it.
If the system points you at one slot but you grabbed from another, the counts will drift, tell the Admin so it can be corrected.
Why it matters: the software gets the order right, but only you can see the actual date on the actual item in your hand. The two together keep the animals safe.

record.field: safety scrap write-off permanent confirm damage repair cannot undo destroy throw away

div.p: Warning: scrapping is permanent. A scrapped item is written off for good, it cannot be brought back into stock. Pause and be sure before you confirm.
Scrapping happens through the Repair flow: an item can only be scrapped while it is in repair. Choosing Scrap means "this can't be fixed and is gone for ever".

ul.li: Can this item be repaired and returned instead? If it's a tool or spare, repair is usually better.
Is the quantity correct? Scrapping 10 when only 1 is broken is hard to reverse.
Has the reason been recorded honestly (broken, expired, contaminated)?

div.p: If Beginner Mode is on, the system will ask you to confirm again, please don't click through it on autopilot.

Throwing something out physically? Record it first. Never quietly bin a broken or expired item. File it through Damage (and Repair/Scrap if needed) so the records match what actually left the building.
Example: a feed sack is contaminated. File a Damage event with reason Contaminated. If it truly can't be saved, scrap it, and now there is a clear, dated record of why it's gone.
Why it matters: every item the trust owns is accounted for. A quiet, unrecorded disposal looks exactly like theft or loss in the books, recording it protects both the trust and you.

record.field: Why can't I move racks into a zone?
move to zone racks floor admin only permission blocked manager organise group reparent

div.p: If the Move to Zone action shows you a message saying it's for Admins only, that's expected. Reorganising the warehouse layout, moving whole racks or floor areas under a zone, is a Manager (Admin) job.

Why it's Admin-only: moving racks around changes the shape of the whole warehouse. It's a planning decision, so it's kept in the hands of the people who set up the layout, to avoid the structure being shuffled by accident during a busy day.
What you can still do as a keeper: all your normal work, receiving, issuing, damage reports, audits, and counts. None of that needs the layout to change.

What to do if racks really do need reorganising: ask the Admin. For them it's a quick job: they pick the racks or floor areas and choose the target zone, and the system reparents them safely (existing stock doesn't move, only the labelling of where things sit).
Example: you notice the pharmacy racks are listed loose instead of under a "Pharmacy" zone. Mention it to the Admin, they can tidy it in under a minute.
Why it matters: keeping layout changes with Admins means the map of the warehouse stays stable and trustworthy for everyone scanning against it.

record.field: Why is a photo required for some issues?
photo required issue measured weight volume kg litre liquid bulk camera proof mandatory

div.p: When you issue an item that is measured by weight or volume, kilograms, litres, cubic metres, the system asks you to attach a photo before you can validate. For items simply counted in pieces, no photo is needed.

Why measured items are different: if you count out 5 bottles, the number is exact. But "3 kg of feed" or "2 litres of medicine" is a judgement, it's easy to pour a little more or less. A quick photo is honest proof of what actually went out.

ul.li: On a phone or tablet: tapping the photo field opens the camera directly, snap the item.
On a desktop: a file picker opens, choose the photo.

div.p: The photo is saved permanently with the issue record, so it's always there in the history.

Example: you issue 4 litres of a fluid supplement. The wizard won't validate until you photograph the container being measured out. Months later, anyone reviewing that issue can see exactly what left.
Tip: you can attach a photo to any issue if you want proof, even counted ones. It's only required for measured items.
Why it matters: for bulk and liquid items, a photo turns a rough figure into a clear, trustworthy record.

record.field: Why won't it let me receive this as a return?
return not returnable scan return refused fluid consumable single use receive blocked kind

div.p: When you use Scan Receipt with the Return entry box ticked, the system only accepts items that are allowed to come back. If an item is refused, it's because it's flagged as not returnable.
What's usually not returnable: fluids, consumables, and single-use items. Once a liquid or a one-time-use item has left the store, it can't sensibly be put back on the shelf as good stock.
The message will name the items and their kind, so you know exactly which lines are the problem.

ul.li: If the item genuinely can't be returned (it's a fluid or consumable), it shouldn't go back into stock. If it's damaged or unusable, file it through the Damage flow instead.
If you believe the item really should be returnable (maybe it's mislabelled), ask the Admin to check the product's WMS Kind and its Returnable flag.

div.p: Example: a worker brings back an unused spanner, fine, it's a returnable tool. But a half-used bottle of teat dip can't go back as stock; that goes through Damage if it's spoiled.
Why it matters: blocking returns of single-use and liquid items keeps spoiled or unusable goods from being logged as fresh, usable stock.

record.field: How do I find where a product is stored?
find product location where is slot search report next to pick walk floor lookup

div.p: You don't need to walk the floor hunting for an item, let the system tell you where it is.

1. Go to WMS → Reports → Where is product X? 2. Search by the product name or its SKU code. 3. The list shows every slot that holds it, with the quantity in each. 4. The slot the system would pick next (oldest stock, or earliest expiry for medicine/feed) is marked "Next to pick".
Click any row to open that slot. From the rack you can open the visual grid to see the slot highlighted on a picture of the rack, handy for guiding a new helper to the right shelf.
Example: a vet asks for dewormer. You search it, see it's in two slots, and the report marks the older batch as "Next to pick". You go straight there instead of opening every drawer.
Tip: the "Next to pick" slot matches what Scan Issue will choose, so following it keeps your physical picking and the system in step.
Why it matters: finding stock from the report saves time, avoids opening the wrong slots, and helps everyone, even a first-day helper, fetch the right item quickly.

record.field: FIFO vs FEFO: which order does the system pick?
fifo fefo difference oldest earliest expiry first in out medicine feed order picking rotation

div.p: When you issue stock, the system decides which units to take first, you don't have to choose. It uses one of two rules:

ul.li: FIFO (First In, First Out) — takes the oldest arrival first. Used for most items. It stops stock sitting forgotten at the back until it goes bad.
FEFO (First Expiry, First Out) — takes the batch that expires soonest first. Used for medicine, feed, fluids, and pooja items, anything where the expiry date matters more than the arrival date.

div.p: For FEFO items, the system can even reach across different batches of the same product to grab the one expiring earliest, so a fresh batch never gets used up before an older one that's about to expire.

ul.li: FIFO: you issue cleaning cloths, the system takes the pack that arrived first.
FEFO: you issue calcium bolus, the system takes the batch expiring this December even if a newer batch arrived more recently.

div.p: What you do: follow the slot the wizard tells you to pick from, and still eyeball the expiry date on medicine/feed (see the FEFO safety note).
Why it matters: the right order means less waste for ordinary stock, and no expired medicine reaching the cows.

record.field: My scan isn't registering, what now?
scan not working scanner cursor barcode nothing happens unknown does not resolve tablet

div.p: If you scan and nothing happens, work through these quick checks, they fix almost every case.
1. Is the cursor in the scan box? The wizard only catches a scan when the Scan here field is active. Tap it once, then scan again. Keep the cursor there and you can scan one item after another.
2. Did the scanner beep? If there's no beep, the scanner didn't read the barcode. Hold it steady, the right distance away, and try a cleaner part of the label.
3. Did you get "Unknown barcode" or "does not resolve to a product"? The barcode isn't linked to anything yet:

ul.li: A vendor carton sticker may need a carton alias set up (this links one carton scan to, say, 24 units). Ask the Admin.
A trust product may need its label printed first.

div.p: 4. Is the slot label faded or missing? Re-print it: WMS → Operations → Slots → tick the slot → menu → Print → WMS Location Labels.
5. On a tablet and the camera/keyboard pops up oddly? Tap the scan field again to refocus, then scan.
Example: a new helper scans and nothing shows. The scan box had lost focus after they tapped elsewhere, one tap back on it and the next scan works.
Why it matters: a scan that doesn't register means stock could end up on a shelf without being recorded, fix the scan before moving the item.

record.field: Why must I pick a Store Keeper on duty, and what if my name isn't there?
store keeper on duty roster name missing add shared login who desk pick required

div.p: On every Scan Issue, Scan Receipt, Damage, and Repair, you must pick the Store Keeper on duty, the actual person running the desk at that moment, from a roster.
Why a roster, not just the login? Several helpers often share one desk login. The roster name records the real human handling the stock, so the audit trail names a person, not just an account.

What if the name I need isn't in the list? It must be added before you can finish. Ask the Admin to add it under Configuration → Store Keepers. It only takes a moment. (If a keeper has left, the Admin retires them by un-ticking "On the roster", which keeps their past records intact without showing them in new dropdowns.)
Example: a temporary helper covers the store for a week. The Admin adds them to the roster on day one; from then on they appear in the dropdown and every action they handle is properly attributed.
Tip: pick the person who is physically handling the stock right now, even if someone else is logged in.
Why it matters: naming the real keeper on duty means responsibility is always clear, which protects honest helpers and makes any problem easy to trace.

record.field: Why can't I cancel this repair order?
repair order cancel blocked in repair done scrapped state stuck cannot draft finish

div.p: Whether you can cancel a repair order depends on what stage it's at, because stock may already have moved.

ul.li: Draft (nothing has moved yet): you can cancel freely.

In repair (the item is at the Repair-Out station): you can't just cancel. Either Mark Done to bring it back to its slot, or Scrap it if it can't be fixed. Cancelling here would leave the item stuck at Repair-Out with no owner.
Done or Scrapped (finished): you can't cancel, because real stock moves were already recorded. If the item needs to leave service again, open a new Damage event.

div.p: What to do when you're blocked: read which state it's in and finish it properly, Mark Done or Scrap for an in-repair item.
Example: you started a repair on a pump, then realised it wasn't needed. Because it's already at Repair-Out, you can't cancel, so you Mark Done to return it to its shelf, leaving a clean record.
Why it matters: a repair order is tied to real stock movements. Forcing a cancel at the wrong time would orphan those moves and leave the books not matching the shelf.

record.field: What does it mean when a location is archived?
archived location inactive hidden retired slot rack restore unarchive missing dropdown

div.p: Archived means a location (a rack, compartment, slot, or floor area) has been set aside, it's hidden from everyday lists and dropdowns, but all its past records are kept.
It's the safe way to retire something you no longer use, instead of deleting it (which would destroy history).

ul.li: An archived slot won't appear when you're choosing where to put stock.
Its old receipts, issues, and audits are still fully there in the records.
It can be brought back any time by un-ticking Archived, nothing is lost.

div.p: "A slot I expected is missing from the list." It may have been archived. Ask the Admin, they can show archived locations and restore it in seconds if it's needed again.
Example: during a tidy-up, three empty corner slots were archived. A month later one is needed again, the Admin simply un-archives it and it reappears, with its full history intact.
Why it matters: archiving keeps your working lists short and clean while never losing the trust's records, the best of both worlds, and far safer than deleting.

record.field: How to add a training video
video record upload youtube vimeo training clip how to class

div.p: You can attach a short video to any help article so a new helper can watch a task instead of only reading about it.

p.b: Best way — upload a clip (works offline):

ul.li: Record a short clip on a phone (landscape, good light). Keep it under 5 minutes and under 50 MB — one task per clip (e.g. "Scanning a receipt").
Save it as MP4 (H.264) if you can — it plays on every device.
Open the article, find Training video (managers only), click Upload a clip, choose the file, and Save.
Add a one-line caption like "Scanning a receipt — 2 min".

div.p: The clip is stored inside the system and is included in every backup. It plays right inside the article — no internet needed, which is ideal for a tablet in the shed.

Other way — paste a YouTube or Vimeo link: if the video is already online, paste its link into Video link instead of uploading. It shows inside the article, but this one needs internet to play. (If you fill both, the uploaded clip wins.)
Tip: keep videos short and focused. Five 1-minute clips beat one 5-minute clip — people find the part they need faster.

record.field: cloud backup google drive off-site offsite upload encrypted copy inventory_backups second copy fire theft

div.p: The cloud backup is a second copy of every encrypted backup, kept in the trust's Google Drive — off the store-room computer, so a fire, theft, or dead disk in the building cannot take the data and its backups together.

It happens automatically: after the daily backup finishes (every afternoon at 4:30 PM), the same encrypted files are uploaded to a Drive folder called Inventory_Backups, organised by year, month, and day. The files are encrypted before they leave the computer, so even someone who got into the Drive account could not read the trust's data.
Why it matters Keeping the only backups next to the live computer protects against a software fault but not against the building. The Drive copy is the "out of the building" safety net.

Real trust example The store-room PC is stolen over a weekend. On a replacement machine, the Admin signs the system back into Google Drive, downloads the newest backup set, and restores it — the trust loses at most one day of records.

ul.li: If the internet is down, the local backup is still made and kept — the Drive upload simply retries on the next run.
A keeper with the Back Up Now permission can send an extra copy any time (see "How to back up to Google Drive now").
Old copies are tidied automatically: daily copies are kept about a month, weekly ones about six months, monthly ones about two years. Manual copies are kept until a Manager decides otherwise.

Never move, rename, or delete anything inside the Inventory_Backups folder in Google Drive. The system can only see the files it created itself; tidying the folder by hand makes backups invisible to it.

record.field: How to back up to Google Drive now
back up now backup now google drive manual extra copy cloud upload safe copy button refresh

div.p: What this is for Sending a safe copy of all WMS data to Google Drive right now, without waiting for the daily 4:30 PM backup — for example after a big receiving day, before a stormy night, or whenever a Manager asks for one. It needs no technical knowledge: one button.

Step by step 1. Open WMS -> Back Up Now. (The menu only appears if you have the Can Run Backup Now permission — Managers always have it; ask the Admin if you need it.) 2. Read the note: nothing is deleted or changed, and you can keep working while it runs. 3. Click Back Up Now. 4. The screen says the backup has started. It takes a few minutes — click Refresh to check, or close the window and come back later. 5. When it finishes, the success screen shows the backup filename, its size in MB, and the time it was uploaded to Google Drive.

If it says "Drive upload pending" The safe copy was made on the server but the internet or Google Drive was not reachable. Nothing is lost — the upload is retried automatically on the next backup run.

ul.li: Double-clicking the button is harmless — the backup never runs twice at once.
Do not go into Google Drive and "tidy" the Inventory_Backups folder. Moving or renaming files there hides them from the system.
This screen only makes backups. Bringing data back is a separate, Manager-only job — if something is wrong with the system, tell a Manager rather than trying to fix it yourself.

div.p: Best practice Run a Back Up Now before anything unusual — a bulk correction, a planned power cut, a machine move — so the newest possible copy is already off the building.

Trust example A festival week ends with hundreds of receipts and issues entered by evening. The keeper clicks Back Up Now before locking up; two minutes later the success screen shows the file, its size, and the Drive upload time. The day's work is safe even if the PC fails overnight.

record.field: Offline cloud backups & the Disaster Recovery page
offline queue pending upload waiting internet reconnect retry abandoned backup disaster recovery DR page google drive validate folder disconnect connect retry now backoff manager

div.p: Who this is for Managers and Admins. It explains what happens to a Google Drive backup when the internet is down, and how to use the Backup & Disaster Recovery page. Store Keepers do not need this — their one job is Back Up Now (see "How to back up to Google Drive now"); the page below is Manager-only.

The promise: the cloud copy can lag, but it can never lose. The local encrypted backup is always made and always kept, whatever the internet is doing. If Google Drive cannot be reached, the day's set is not thrown away — it is queued and uploaded automatically the moment the connection comes back. Nobody has to remember to retry it.

ul.li: Waiting for internet — the local backup is safe on the computer; the Drive upload is parked. As soon as the box is back online, an hourly check sends it up. No action needed.

Automatic retries with a cooling-off gap — if an upload keeps failing, the system waits a little longer between each attempt (15 minutes, then 30, then an hour, and so on, up to once a day) so it never hammers a flaky line.

Abandoned — only after many attempts over about two weeks does a set give up and show as abandoned. That means a real, lasting problem (the Google sign-in expired, the Drive is full, or the internet was down for a long time). The system stays healthy-with-a-warning, never "critical": the local backup is still safe.

div.p: The Backup & Disaster Recovery page Open WMS → Configuration → Backup & Disaster Recovery. From top to bottom it shows:

ul.li: Connection — whether the trust is signed in to Google Drive, and which Gmail account. It shows only whether the credentials are present ("configured" / "present"), never the secret values themselves — by design, the page cannot read or store a password or token.
Backup folder — paste a Google Drive folder link and press Validate Folder to confirm the system can write there.
Schedule & Retention — the daily backup time and how long copies are kept.
Offline upload queue — how many sets are pending, waiting for internet, or abandoned, plus the last successful upload and the last error. This is your at-a-glance health for the cloud tier.
Retry Now — a button that tries the queued uploads immediately instead of waiting for the hourly check. Safe to press any time.

p.b: What to do when something is wrong

ul.li: "Waiting for internet" sets — usually nothing; they clear themselves when the line is back. Press Retry Now to test at once.

"Auth expired" — the Google sign-in lapsed. Ask the Admin to re-run the one-time sign-in at the server (scripts\setup-gdrive-auth.ps1); the backlog then uploads on its own. Connecting cannot be done from this web page — Google opens a browser on the server for it.

"Abandoned" sets — fix the cause (sign-in, full Drive, or a long outage), then click Back Up Now: a fresh copy uploads cleanly and the warning clears. Nothing was lost — the local encrypted copy is still on the computer.
This page never restores anything. Bringing data back is a separate, console-only, Manager-supervised job (see the restore guide). The web app has no "restore" button on purpose.
Do not paste any Google password, client secret, or token anywhere on this page — there is no field for it, and there should never be one.
Do not "tidy" the Inventory_Backups folder in Google Drive; moving or renaming files there hides them from the system.

div.p: Trust example A monsoon storm knocks out the broadband for two days. Each afternoon the 4:30 PM backup still runs and is kept on the store-room PC; the Drive uploads queue as waiting. When the line is restored on the third morning, the hourly check quietly uploads all three days' sets within minutes — the Manager sees the queue empty itself and the last-upload time go green, with no lost data and nothing to do by hand.
